Findings reveal a shift away from X (formerly Twitter) and a stronger focus on more outspoken audiovisual platforms such as TikTok for news sourcing and diffusion purposes, while ascribing growing relevance to LinkedIn and even traditional text messages. Politicians’ messages are perceived as steering away from overt political messages, feeding into the ongoing debate about the depoliticization of political communication.

item.title: The power of conversational writing style: Examining the influence of sourcing and writing style on credibility in community journalism
item.dc:creator: Chun Hong Tse, Kecheng Fang
item.description:
Journalism · Chun Hong Tse, Kecheng Fang

Topics: Journalism, News credibility, Citizen journalism, Narrative persuasion

This article revisits the issue of the credibility of citizen journalism in the context of community news. By unpacking its two major reporting characteristics — sourcing from citizens and conversational writing style — this study contributes to our understanding of what makes citizen journalism trustworthy. A 2 (sourcing: elite vs citizen) × 2 (writing style: conversational vs professional) between-subjects experiment ( N = 311) was conducted in Taiwan in late January 2024. Results showed that conversational writing style was considered more credible and more narratively transported than professional journalistic writing. Besides, media skepticism moderated the relationship between conversational writing style and narrative transportation. This implies that, at least concerning community topics, conversational writing style emerges as the critical factor enabling citizen journalism to win trust among the public. Furthermore, results suggest a need to reconsider the rigid professional journalistic norms in certain settings, as the traditional reporting style creates a distance with readers and may be unsuitable for addressing personal-related or emotionally charged topics such as community news and disaster news.

item.title: More Clickbait, But Fewer Shares? Unpacking the Relationship Between Multimodal Sensationalism and Online User Engagement
item.dc:creator: Xucheng Cao, Shuhua Zhou, Jinye Zhu, Xiaohui Wang
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Xucheng Cao, Shuhua Zhou, Jinye Zhu, Xiaohui Wang

Topics: Multimodal analysis, Social media engagement, Journalism, Content analysis

This study examined multimodal sensationalism by analyzing how textual and visual sensationalist features embedded in video headlines and thumbnails relate to user engagement. Using a hybrid human-large language model content analysis, we identified 15 sensationalist features across 1,100 trending videos from Douyin. The results show that legacy news outlets used fewer textual sensationalist elements, particularly Internet slang, hashtags, and positive emotions, than non-journalistic producers. Additionally, visual sensationalist features exhibited an inverted U-shaped relationship with user engagement. These findings advance understanding of the nonlinear and modality-specific effects of sensationalism and offer practical insights into the optimal use of multimodal sensationalism on social media.

item.title: Are they virtue-signalling or sincere? The impact of perceived motives on the effectiveness of online collective action
item.dc:creator: Lisette Yip, Emma F. Thomas, Hawa Muhammad Farid, M. Noor Tahir
item.description:
New Media & Society · Lisette Yip, Emma F. Thomas, Hawa Muhammad Farid, M. Noor Tahir

Topics: Online collective action, Social movements, Perceived motives, Social identity

Social media is an important tool used by supporters of modern social movements to persuade others to participate. However, people who engage in online collective action often face speculation about their motives and may be perceived as acting for self-serving reasons. How do these perceptions impact the effectiveness of collective action? In three experiments ( N = 916), participants viewed posts (Study 1) or an immersive social media feed (Studies 2–3) where a user encouraged them to take action for a political cause. They stated that they acted out of genuine concern (autonomous motivation), to avoid guilt and social disapproval (controlled motivation), or did not specify (baseline). Participants who viewed controlled-motivated posts perceived the user as less autonomously motivated and were therefore less likely to socially identify as supporters or take collective action. Thus, movements will be more effective at mobilising (online) support when they are seen to arise from autonomous motives.

item.title: Cross-platformization: How U.S. right-leaning media curate their posts on Twitter and Truth Social
item.dc:creator: Josephine Lukito, Yini Zhang, Bin Chen, Stephen Prochaska, Meredith L. Pruden, Yunkang Yang, Wei Zhong, Megan A. Brown, Ross Dahlke, Jason Greenfield
item.description:
New Media & Society · Josephine Lukito, Yini Zhang, Bin Chen, Stephen Prochaska, Meredith L. Pruden, Yunkang Yang, Wei Zhong, Megan A. Brown, Ross Dahlke, Jason Greenfield

Topics: Social media platforms, Political polarization, Platform affordances, News organizations

This study examines how seven right-leaning media organizations utilize cross-platformization strategies to reach audiences across multiple platforms; in this case, Twitter and Truth Social. Focusing on both content volume and story packaging, we collect right-leaning media organizations’ social media posts and content from the 2022 U.S. midterm election. Combining computational and qualitative methods, we find that outlets posted only a small share of total stories across the two platforms and were selective in their content, often posting only on Twitter or Truth Social. For content posted on both platforms, the outlets posted content that ideologically aligned with the users of that platform. More specifically, right-leaning outlets on Truth Social tailored their posts to ideologically aligned users.

item.title: Disappearing Voices, Emerging Resistance: Journalism, Language, and Social Inequality in the U.S.-Mexico Borderlands
item.dc:creator: Jéssica Retis, Susan Barnett, Liliana Lopez Ruelas
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Jéssica Retis, Susan Barnett, Liliana Lopez Ruelas

Topics: Journalism, News deserts, Community engagement, Digital inequality

This article examines how linguistic, geographic, and racial inequalities shape journalism in the U.S.-Mexico borderlands. Focusing on Southern Arizona, it analyzes the rise of two community-driven Spanish-language news startups following the closure of the city’s only Spanish-language newspaper. Emerging in connection with a bilingual journalism initiative at a local university, these projects developed through collaborative research, community engagement, and newsroom experimentation aimed at addressing gaps in local news coverage. Drawing on research-action practices, collaborative research, and self-ethnography, the study examines how marginalized communities resist exclusion by producing culturally relevant media. It situates these efforts within broader discussions of news deserts, institutional inequality, and the systemic neglect of linguistic minorities, offering insight into how grassroots journalism—and the institutional spaces that can help incubate it—can challenge dominant media norms and reimagine local news in underserved, multilingual communities.

item.title: Being journalists on social media: Contrasting professionals’ self-perceptions to role expectations among adolescents
item.dc:creator: Vasco Avides Moreira, Darian Harff
item.description:
Journalism · Vasco Avides Moreira, Darian Harff

Topics: Journalistic roles, Social media, Journalism, Professional norms

On social media, efforts by individual journalists to share news with audiences may be a viable response to personality-driven news presentation coming from peripheral actors like influencers, who are increasingly popular information sources for adolescents. Yet, when using social media to disseminate content, journalists may risk backlash, especially when innovative approaches represent a deviation from traditional journalistic norms. Drawing on expectancy violations theory and semi-structured qualitative interviews conducted among Portuguese journalists ( N = 7) and adolescents ( N = 20), we contrasted professionals’ own perceptions of being journalists on social media to adolescents’ role expectations. Findings showed that adolescents generally prefer journalists to be personal and independent when presenting news on social media, though they also recognized that journalists may in this context be bound by institutional rules. Similarly, journalists highlighted perceived pressure coming from news organizations and licensing bodies to abide by professional standards, even when using their private social media. Despite seeing value in adopting a ‘newsfluencer’-like role, journalists’ need to negotiate between various interests and expectations represents one of the main hurdles that prevents them from establishing a clear presence on these platforms – and may explain low attraction to journalistic sources on social media among adolescents.

item.title: When even empathy would be enough – Representation of homelessness in the Czech mainstream media during Christmas
item.dc:creator: Vojtěch Dvořák
item.description:
Journalism · Vojtěch Dvořák

Topics: Media representation, News coverage, Media framing, Media coverage

Homelessness remains one of the most persistent and complex societal issues globally, and the media play a significant role in shaping both representations of and public attitudes toward this marginalized population. This study presents a thematic analysis of Czech mainstream news coverage of homelessness during three consecutive Christmas periods (2022, 2023, and 2024). While Christmas coverage might be expected to foreground empathy, humanization, or solidarity more strongly than routine reporting, the analysis shows that such elements remained relatively marginal in the Czech material examined here. The findings reveal a persistent scarcity of solidarity and empathy, with media portrayals frequently reinforcing harmful stereotypes rather than challenging them. The study concludes that substantial changes in media discourse are necessary to promote more accurate and just representations of homelessness in the Czech and possibly further Eastern European context.

item.title: Investigating Conditional Macro-Level Media Effects Over a Long-Term: How Crisis Periods Moderate the Effects of Suicide Coverage on Suicide Rate Change (1861–2007)
item.dc:creator: Christina Viehmann, Stefan Geiß, Manina Mestas, Oliver Quiring, Florian Arendt
item.description:
Communication Research · Christina Viehmann, Stefan Geiß, Manina Mestas, Oliver Quiring, Florian Arendt

Topics: Media effects, Suicide reporting, Long-term media effects, Computational text analysis

How does media shape society over decades, and does its effect vary depending on the societal atmosphere or zeitgeist ? While theoretically important, there is a lack of systematic empirical evidence on conditional long-term macro-level media effects. We propose a broader framework to study such effects and demonstrate its applicability for the “Werther effect” in the UK. More specifically, we investigate whether media coverage of suicides in a newspaper of record is linked to suicide rates and whether this link changes during societal crises. For this, we combine suicide data with a large-scale automated content analysis of crisis and suicide reporting in The Times over a century (1861-2007). Our analysis shows that increased suicide reporting is associated with higher suicide rates, but only during crisis periods. The results are consistent with a conditional Werther effect and may offer one piece of the larger puzzle of long-term macro-level media influences on society.

item.title: Inequality Within the Mobile System: Understanding the Third-Level Digital Divide Through Adverse Digital Incorporation in Rural China
item.dc:creator: Jingke Lin, Jianjie Tao
item.description:
Mobile Media & Communication · Jingke Lin, Jianjie Tao

Topics: Digital divide, Mobile media, Digital inequality, Digital labor

As mobile media rapidly expand in the rural Global South, digital divide research is shifting from an exclusion-based to an inclusion-based perspective. Drawing on Heeks’ “adverse digital incorporation” framework and ethnographic fieldwork in rural China, this article conceptualizes the third-level digital divide, which refers to the unequal outcomes and disparate dividends derived from information and communication technologies, as the unequal extraction of value resulting from power imbalances within the mobile system. The study reveals that this adverse incorporation constitutes two closed loops of value inequality. On the one hand, smartphones break spatiotemporal boundaries to extract value through the commodification of private time, legibility and labor control, and risk-cost shifting. On the other hand, while rural residents employ strategic digital disconnection as a form of everyday resistance, which results in marginalization and reinforces value inequality. Consequently, it is essential to go beyond technical provision to enable rural residents to transform from passive content consumers into active value producers and to rebalance power within the mobile system.

item.title: Relationship Between Cyberbullying and Social Anxiety, School Refusal, and Academic Goals in Adolescents
item.dc:creator: Elizabeth Cañas, Mari Carmen Martínez-Monteagudo, Beatriz Delgado, Esther Rubio, David Aparisi
item.description:
Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking · Elizabeth Cañas, Mari Carmen Martínez-Monteagudo, Beatriz Delgado, Esther Rubio, David Aparisi

Topics: Cyberbullying, Social anxiety, School refusal, Academic goals

Examining the associations between cyberbullying involvement and psychoeducational factors may contribute to a better understanding of adolescents’ experiences in online peer contexts. The aim of this study was to examine the associations between cyberbullying involvement, considering the roles of cybervictim, cyberaggressor, and cyberbystander, and three psychoeducational constructs: social anxiety, school refusal, and academic goals. A total of 1,412 Spanish secondary and upper-secondary school students aged 12–18 years ( M = 14.36, SD = 1.65) completed a battery of questionnaires assessing cyberbullying, social anxiety, school refusal, and academic goals. Three independent binary logistic regression models were conducted, one for each cyberbullying role, using the psychoeducational dimensions as predictors. The findings showed that the associations varied according to both the psychoeducational dimension and the cyberbullying role. In particular, Discomfort and avoidance in social situations in general was positively associated with cybervictimization, cyberaggression, and cyberbystanding, whereas other dimensions of social anxiety showed negative associations with some roles. Avoidance of stimuli or situations related to the school context was positively associated with the three cyberbullying roles. Learning and Achievement goals were negatively associated with cybervictimization, cyberaggression, and cyberbystanding, whereas Social reinforcement goals were positively associated with cyberaggression. These findings highlight the multidimensional nature of the associations between psychoeducational factors and cyberbullying involvement and support the consideration of individual and educational variables in the design of prevention and intervention strategies during adolescence.

item.title: Sex, Romance, or Recreation? An Experiment Testing the Effects of Cannabis Brand-generated Social Media Ads on College Students’ Expectancies and Intentions to Use Cannabis Prior to Sex
item.dc:creator: Jessica Fitts Willoughby, Stacey J. T. Hust, Leticia Couto, Jiayu Li, Soojung Kang
item.description:
Communication Research · Jessica Fitts Willoughby, Stacey J. T. Hust, Leticia Couto, Jiayu Li, Soojung Kang

Topics: Cannabis marketing, Social media advertising, Sexual scripts, Health communication

Sexual and romantic scripts are used to market cannabis products, now legal for adult-use in several U.S. states. We conducted an online experiment ( N = 747) examining the impact of viewing brand-generated social media posts promoting cannabis that included sexual, romantic, and non-sexual non-romantic recreational scripts among college students in Washington state. Increased perceptions that ads suggested cannabis enhances sex were associated with higher sex-related cannabis expectancies. Among men, wishful identification was associated with lower sexual risk expectancies among those who viewed sexual scripts and a greater likelihood of intending to use cannabis before sex among those who viewed sexual or romantic scripts. Among women, perceiving that ads suggested cannabis enhances sex was associated with a greater likelihood of intending to use cannabis before sex, whereas perceiving that ads suggested cannabis impacts sexual consent was associated with a lower likelihood of intending to use cannabis before sex. Additionally, wishful identification among women was associated with a greater likelihood of intending to use cannabis before sex. Findings highlight associations between perceptions of brand-generated social media posts, expectancies, and intentions to use cannabis before sex among college students and identify mechanisms through which effects may occur.

item.title: Framing the regional frontlines: challenges, ethical dilemmas and experiences of Journalists in Northeast India
item.dc:creator: Sayan Dey
item.description:
Journalism · Sayan Dey

Topics: Journalistic role perceptions, Professional norms, Journalism studies, Digital journalism

This article investigates how journalists in Northeast India negotiate objectivity, ethics and journalistic role perceptions while covering conflicts in geo-politically sensitive and digitally mediated settings. Drawing on eight in-depth interviews, this study reveals how journalists navigate safety concerns, emotional connections and platform logics that increasingly affect their workflows. Employing Framing Theory and Role Theory, the paper highlights three interconnected dimensions: journalists’ reflexive negotiation between emotional attachment and professional neutrality, increasing influence of platform logics and analytics in editorial processes; and contextual restrictions arising from state control and linguistic hegemonies within the Indian national media landscape. The findings demonstrate that in conflict settings, journalistic objectivity is contextually negotiated rather than being universally fixed, highlighting moral sensitivities and hybrid professionalism in peripheral media settings. By examining the lived realities of journalists; the study contributes to de-Westernised discourses in Journalism Studies and explains how journalists in parts of the Global South, especially in conflict-sensitive and marginalised territories, reimagine journalistic ethics and agency amid political, cultural and technological challenges.

item.title: From “water, food, energy” to electoral legitimacy: media discourse and symbolic meaning-making in Romania’s 2024 election crisis
item.dc:creator: Antonio Amuza, Dan-Niculae PODARU
item.description:
Journalism · Antonio Amuza, Dan-Niculae PODARU

Topics: Populism, Political communication, Media framing, Discourse analysis

This article examines how populist political legitimacy is discursively constructed through semiotic framing in a context of democratic instability. Focusing on Romania’s 2024 presidential crisis, the study analyses how nationalist and anti-establishment meanings are produced, circulated, and recontextualized across digital and traditional media environments. Drawing on semiotic theory and critical discourse approaches, the article explores how recurring symbolic elements, such as sovereignty , moral purity , and elemental resources , operate as indexical signs that connect individual grievances to broader ideological narratives. The analysis combines qualitative discourse analysis of candidate communication, computational analysis of 10,556 news articles, and post-electoral survey data ( N = 572) collected immediately after the first round of voting. The analysis shows how discursive strategies contribute to processes of political legitimation by framing power relations in affective and moral terms rather than procedural or institutional ones. Empirical survey data are used to contextualize how these symbolic repertoires circulated across fragmented media environments and were associated with differentiated patterns of electoral alignment. The findings highlight the central role of media discourse and symbolic framing in shaping political legitimacy, polarization, and interpretive authority within contemporary hybrid media systems, offering insights into the symbolic mechanisms through which legitimacy is negotiated in post-socialist societies.

item.title: Authoritative Yet Conditionally Cohesive: The Cohesion Dynamics of Journalistic (Non-) Authority on Chinese TikTok (Douyin)
item.dc:creator: Peng Xiao, Wen Shi, Yangkun Huang
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Peng Xiao, Wen Shi, Yangkun Huang

Topics: Journalism, Short-form video, Platform affordances, Social media algorithms

The rise of algorithmic curation challenges the traditional authority of journalism. Focusing on Douyin, this study employed agent-based testing and temporal network analysis to examine how recommendation systems generate network cohesion around Chinese state and non-state media. Results revealed that state media’s cohesive power stemmed from news, whereas cohesion around non-state media was sustained by non-news content. However, for both media types, the cohesion generated by news showed a significant decline over time, and this trend varied by topic. These findings suggest that, beyond mere institutional status, strategic content adaptation is fundamental to building network cohesion in algorithmic environments.

item.title: Ambivalent algorithms, fragile connectedness: How algorithm awareness facets shape responsiveness and insensitivity on TikTok
item.dc:creator: Dragoș M. Obreja
item.description:
New Media & Society · Dragoș M. Obreja

Topics: Algorithm awareness, Social media algorithms, TikTok, Social connectedness

This study examines how distinct facets of algorithm awareness are associated with perceived algorithm responsiveness (PAR), perceived algorithm insensitivity (PAI), and social connectedness on TikTok. I draw on the algorithm responsiveness process and also treat algorithm awareness as four distinct dimensions (content filtering, automated decision‑making, human–algorithm interplay (HAI), ethical concerns) to examine how each dimension is differentially associated with PAR and PAI and, in turn, with feelings of inclusion and belonging. Using survey data from 305 TikTok users and structural equation modeling, I show that user‑agency‑oriented dimensions, particularly filtering and HAI, are indirectly associated with connectedness via higher responsiveness and lower insensitivity. By contrast, automation operates as an ambivalent structure: it boosts responsiveness yet is negatively associated with connectedness, marking a boundary condition for personalization. Platforms should pair automation disclosures with clearer user recourse, traceable feedback, and human review in high-stakes contexts.

item.title: The year is a dropdown menu: Platformed provenance and the viral afterlives of AI-generated retro music
item.dc:creator: Matilde Catanese
item.description:
New Media & Society · Matilde Catanese

Topics: Generative AI, Platform affordances, Misinformation, Digital media

This article examines how generative AI media becomes believable and shareable when it is packaged as a rediscovered archive and distributed through commercial platforms. Drawing on multi-sited digital ethnography, targeted platform walkthroughs, and cross-platform trace analysis of a viral “lost song” circulating in Italy in 2025, I show how listeners in this case mobilized sonic cues and platform metadata, including release dates and credits, as practical evidence. I use metadata realism to describe everyday reliance on database fields as documentary testimony, and provenance play for situated practices of verification and narration through which people negotiate synthetic pasts. After public debunking, circulation continued through humorous and artistic reframings, while verification itself became part of the artifact’s social life. The analysis foregrounds platformed provenance and considers what the case implies for synthetic media governance and content credentials.

item.title: News for connection, status and belonging: Exploring the social currency of local news
item.dc:creator: Jee Young Lee, Sora Park, Janet Fulton
item.description:
New Media & Society · Jee Young Lee, Sora Park, Janet Fulton

Topics: Local news, Social currency, News consumption, Social influence

This paper explores the perception of social currency as a distinct value within local news consumption among audiences. Social currency refers to the value individuals derive from engaging with and sharing news content within their social networks, allowing them to connect, express identity and signal awareness. Drawing on a large-scale mixed-methods study of local news audiences in Australia (survey: n = 7919; interviews and focus groups: n = 84), this study operationalised key dimensions of social currency using factor analysis. The findings confirm that social currency is a separate and measurable construct, distinct from traditional news motivations. It is significantly higher among younger people, men, urban residents and those from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds, reflecting how news consumption intersects with social interaction, identity expression and symbolic practices of everyday life.

item.title: Epistemic governance in journalism: Editorial, algorithmic, and regulatory logics in a contested epistemic space
item.dc:creator: Aina Errando
item.description:
Journalism · Aina Errando

Topics: Journalistic practice, Algorithmic curation, Platform governance, News credibility

Journalism’s epistemic authority—its capacity to produce and legitimate public knowledge—is shaped beyond the newsroom. Editorial judgment now operates alongside algorithmic systems that structure visibility and distribution, and regulatory frameworks that impose obligations and safeguards. Although scholarship has examined these domains separately, it lacks an integrated account of how epistemic authority is enacted across them. This article develops an Epistemic Governance Framework that conceptualizes journalism’s authority as a governed outcome of three interdependent logics: editorial, algorithmic, and regulatory. Drawing on Actor-Network Theory, the article treats these logics as overlapping sociotechnical arrangements and proposes their intersection as a Contested Epistemic Space in which competing criteria of visibility, credibility, and accountability are negotiated. The article contributes a framework for analyzing how journalistic authority is assembled, contested, and stabilized, and outlines implications for future empirical research and normative debate on the governance of public knowledge.

item.title: Reporting the periphery: War and peace journalism in the coverage of the 2023 Manipur violence
item.dc:creator: A. Asou Chiiste, Paokholun Hangsing, Xavier G. Marak
item.description:
Journalism · A. Asou Chiiste, Paokholun Hangsing, Xavier G. Marak

Topics: Peace journalism, News framing, Media representation, Content analysis

This study examines national media coverage of ethnic conflict through the lens of peace journalism, focusing on the 2023 Manipur conflict in Northeast India – a region often absent from national news discourse. While peace journalism research has expanded across diverse conflict contexts, scholarship foregrounding marginalized peripheral regions remains limited. Drawing on Galtung’s peace journalism framework and center-periphery theory as complementary analytical lenses, the study analyzed 360 news reports published by three leading Indian national news outlets from May to October 2023. The analysis identified the prevalence of war and peace frames across outlets and employed a novel indicator co-occurrence approach to assess the depth of violence coverage. Results show a clear dominance of war frames, with emphasis on immediate developments, visible effects of violence, and elite sources, while peace-oriented indicators such as the examination of causes, civilian voices, and solution orientation were systematically underrepresented. An indicator-level analysis further revealed that while outlets diverge in framing orientation and language use, they converge in their failure to engage with contextual depth. A key implication is that journalistic neutrality alone does not necessarily prevent, and may inadvertently contribute to, the epistemic marginalization of peripheral communities in national conflict reporting.

item.title: “Enthusiasts, Not Professionals”: Journalists’ Experiences of Precarity in Serbia’s Hybrid Regime
item.dc:creator: Igor Išpanović, Čedomir Markov
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Igor Išpanović, Čedomir Markov

Topics: Journalism, Journalistic practice, Professional norms, Political communication

Precarity has become a defining feature of the contemporary journalistic labor market worldwide. Drawing on 20 in-depth interviews with journalists in Serbia, we explore the tension between precarity and professional journalistic aspirations. Although participants understood precarious working conditions primarily in economic terms (e.g., low wages and limited job opportunities), their accounts suggest that labor (in)security is distributed according to political rather than market logic. Some respond to these pressures by adopting nondemocratic journalistic practices or by adjusting their professional values, while others embrace precarity as a mark of professional integrity and a condition for practicing journalism in a hybrid regime.

item.title: “This is how journalism has always been done”: White neutrality, newsroom norms, and an AI intervention in source diversification
item.dc:creator: Gavin Adamson, Asmaa Malik, Shari Okeke, Jisele Bayley-Hay
item.description:
Journalism · Gavin Adamson, Asmaa Malik, Shari Okeke, Jisele Bayley-Hay

Topics: Journalistic practice, Artificial intelligence in journalism, Newsroom practices, Journalistic roles

This study draws on interviews with 12 journalists in a Canadian newsroom to examine how they understand source diversification, how they perceive AI-based source-tracking technology, and how their reflections illuminate discourse on race and accountability in journalism. Based on semi-structured interviews conducted after a demonstration of the technology, the analysis identifies the motivations and barriers shaping source diversification, including professional norms, representational goals, time constraints, and institutional culture. Reporters express commitments to inclusive sourcing, but remain constrained by routines that privilege official voices, anticipated by research analysis like framing and indexing theories. Participants describe the AI tool, which quantitatively scores sources according to their relationship to societal power structures, as a potential catalyst for reflective practice and accountability. They also suggest the technology may sit uneasily within professional norms. The study is contextualized in research about role performance and race in newsrooms. Finally, this AI-based source-tracking technology resituates journalism within a Bourdieusian field, pulled toward social and cultural capital in relation to structural racism.

item.title: “Talk as if it doesn’t impact you”: Black TV journalist’s experiences covering BLM protests in the U.S.
item.dc:creator: Kaitlin C. Miller, Samantha Kocan
item.description:
Journalism · Kaitlin C. Miller, Samantha Kocan

Topics: Journalistic roles, Intersectionality, Emotional labor, Journalism

This article explores the effects that covering Black Lives Matter protests had on Black TV journalists. Using in-depth semi-structured interviews with 14 Black journalists across the U.S., this study investigates their experiences covering BLM protests, as well as how supported they felt by their organizations/supervisors. Through qualitative interviews, research shows that Black journalists felt torn between their identities as both journalists and Black—navigating objective reporting with a deep emotional empathy for protestors. Moreover, they did not feel supported by their news organizations, who did not prioritize their well-being, and who tailored news coverage for a White audience. The intersectional implications of this are discussed as well as concerns about emotional labor.

item.title: Investigating under fire: Journalistic challenges in Afghanistan’s Republic era (2001–2021)
item.dc:creator: Ahmad Jahed Mushtaq
item.description:
Journalism · Ahmad Jahed Mushtaq

Topics: Investigative journalism, Journalistic practice, News production, Media systems

Investigative journalism plays a vital role in exposing wrongdoing. This study examines the practices and challenges of investigative reporting in Afghanistan during the Republic era (2001–2021). Drawing on in-depth interviews with fifteen investigative journalists from leading television networks, it applies the Hierarchy of Influences model to analyze how multiple levels of pressure shaped investigative reporting in a conflict-affected context. The findings reveal that investigative reporting was constrained across the individual, routines, organizational, extramedia, and social system levels. At the individual level, journalists engaged in anticipatory self-censorship. At the routines level, newsroom practices and narration strategies reflected the normalization of insecurity in everyday work. Organizational pressures, including financial constraints, media dependency, and editorial control, undermined investigative practice. At the extramedia level, pressures from government officials, armed groups, and other actors created an unpredictable reporting environment. At the social system level, weak rule of law, limited enforcement, restricted access to information, and cultural norms narrowed the scope of investigative reporting. The study extends the Hierarchy of Influences model by demonstrating that macro-level pressures converged at the story-conception stage, producing temporal compression across levels of influence. At the same time, journalists exercised negotiated agency through adaptive strategies that enabled investigative journalism to persist despite severe constraints.

item.title: Can democracy speak under AI-driven visibility? Toward an affective–algorithmic reworking of the spiral of silence
item.dc:creator: Lourenço Silva Ferreira
item.description:
European Journal of Communication · Lourenço Silva Ferreira

Topics: Spiral of silence, Algorithmic curation, Political communication, Populism

This article offers a critical theoretical reassessment of the conditions shaping political expression and its boundaries within algorithmically mediated publics, examining how artificial intelligence–driven infrastructures of visibility, intertwined with affective dynamics, alter the conditions under which opinions acquire public presence and come to be perceived as legitimate to express. The argument is illustrated through a case-based analysis of highly visible user interactions surrounding posts by the Portuguese populist leader André Ventura across Facebook, TikTok and X, which serves to explore how different socio-technical environments give rise to distinct climates of opinion. Revisiting the Spiral of Silence theory from the perspective of contemporary platform environments, the article argues that silencing is no longer adequately explained primarily through interpersonal fear of isolation, but must instead be understood as emerging from the interplay between algorithmically structured visibility and affectively charged interaction. On this basis, the article reconceptualises the Spiral of Silence as an affective–algorithmic process and contributes to debates in communication theory and digital political communication, while asking whether, and under what conditions, democracy can still be said to speak when publicness itself is algorithmically organised.

item.title: Less Effort to Believe and More Effort to Disbelieve: Examining the Interplay between News-Finds-Me and Affective Polarization in Political Fake News Susceptibility in the United States
item.dc:creator: Yu Tian, Lars Willnat, Baohua Zhou
item.description:
Communication Research · Yu Tian, Lars Willnat, Baohua Zhou

Topics: Fake news, Affective polarization, Political polarization, Selective exposure

Drawing upon an online survey of 719 US adult partisans incorporating response latency data, we connected News-Finds-Me (NFM) to the partisan-motivated reasoning literature and theorized it as a consensus-based mode of news exposure that leads to different news-processing pathways, where the vested news-processing effort depends on whether the political falsehood aligns with one’s partisan identity and surrounding majority opinion. Individual-level analysis and headline-level modeling jointly illuminated the asymmetric interplay between NFM and affective polarization. In partisan-consistent scenarios, high-NFM users devoted limited processing time, falling short of cognitive effort to enable affect-laden, directional believing of partisan-consistent fake news. However, when challenged by partisan inconsistency, high-NFM users dedicated significantly more processing time, which exacerbated the relationship between affective polarization and refutation of partisan-inconsistent falsehoods. Contrarily, such an effort discrepancy, widely documented in the partisan-motivated reasoning literature, was weakened or reversed for low-NFM individuals. Extending the “Effort-Reinforces-Directional-Reasoning” thesis to fake news vulnerability, our findings underscore the paradoxical interplay between NFM and affective polarization: while NFM and affective polarization deviate people from active news-seeking and accuracy-oriented reasoning, their joint dynamics form a type of group thinking that reduces vulnerability to partisan falsehoods—even those aligned with one’s partisan attachments.

item.title: Audible, Spotify, YouTube & Co.: The German Digital Audiobook Market in the Context of Platformization
item.dc:creator: Sven Stollfuß
item.description:
New Media & Society · Sven Stollfuß

Topics: Platformization, Digital media, Streaming services, Digital platforms

This article examines the contemporary digital audiobook through the lens of platformization and develops a conceptual framework for understanding platformized audiobook culture. Drawing on an integrative review of interdisciplinary scholarship, supplemented by market reports, industry statistics, and audience studies, it uses the German audiobook market as an analytically illuminating example through which broader processes of platformization can be explored. The article situates audiobooks within wider transformations of everyday digital media practices, highlighting the shift from physical formats toward downloads and subscription-based streaming services. Conceptually, it distinguishes platformized audiobook culture from digital audiobook culture through two complementary analytical perspectives adapted from book studies, digital publishing, and media and communication studies: an integrative platform model and a data-environment model of streaming services. Building on this synthesis, the article proposes an ecosystem model of platformized audiobook culture to support future theoretical and empirical research.

item.title: The intended and unintended affordances of post-separation parenting apps
item.dc:creator: Michelle A. Irving, Jenny L. Davis
item.description:
New Media & Society · Michelle A. Irving, Jenny L. Davis

Topics: Platform affordances, Domestic violence, Digital communication, Interpersonal communication

Little research has examined the role of specific technologies in relationships characterised by unequal power, such as those which underpin post-separation domestic and family violence. Drawing on the mechanisms and conditions framework of affordances and the methods of feature analysis, this study analyses 32 post-separation parenting apps along with in-depth interviews with 18 Australian victim–survivors who used these platforms with a perpetrator. We identify intended outcomes embedded in app design and contrast them with unintended outcomes emerging in practice. Analysis revealed that the design and promotional materials of the apps influence their use as a reinforcer of litigious mindsets and actions. This combination appears to change user behaviours, leading to communication becoming anticipatory and strategic with mixed outcomes.

item.title: #BlackExcellence and #BlackGirlMagic are for all of us: Black influencers’ rejection of neoliberal logics and post-feminist discourses of entrepreneurship
item.dc:creator: Wesley E. Stevens
item.description:
New Media & Society · Wesley E. Stevens

Topics: Social media influencers, Digital labor, Intersectionality, Platform affordances

Situated within feminist media communication studies, this project uses critical technocultural discourse analysis to examine how #BlackExcellence emerges as a form of “digital Black practice” among Black women influencers and users. This study is framed within the context of the George Floyd protests in 2020 and 2021 as mainstream media outlets appropriated Black Excellence rhetoric in columns, listicles, and videos following this watershed moment. Analyses of popular press articles about Black influencers, discourse about race and labor on #BlackTumblr, influencer content on Instagram and YouTube, and interviews with Black influencers comprise the dataset. By leveraging intersectional platform affordances and racialized erotic capital, Black influencers subvert neoliberal and post-feminist logics undergirding digital labor by virtue of the racialized work they are expected to perform, challenging exceptionalist rhetoric. I argue that Black influencers’ uniquely racialized, gendered work contests the assumption that influencer labor is a natural outgrowth of neoliberal conditions.

item.title: Human versus AI news anchors: A survey study on audience satisfaction and the emotional connection
item.dc:creator: Yuan Ji
item.description:
Journalism · Yuan Ji

Topics: Artificial intelligence in journalism, Audience perception, Audience engagement, Trust

As artificial intelligence becomes widely used in the digital newsroom, AI virtual anchors have been widely accepted, leading to the alteration of the traditional model of news presentation. In this study, perceptions, satisfaction and emotional attachment of the Chinese news viewers to the AI news anchors. A questionnaire of 343 Beijing residents was collected as primary data. Frameworks like Diffusion of Innovations (DoI) and Social Construction of Technology (SCOT) have been core theoretical foundation. The findings suggest that credibility scepticism, moderate acceptance, and low emotional connectivity with AI anchors were high. The perceived authenticity and emotional connectivity had a significant correlation with the overall satisfaction of the audience, and the acceptance patterns were mediated by demographic factors. Human communicative values such as trust, emotional appeal, and responsibility proved to be the most crucial factors in determining the interests of the audience. The implications of these findings can be applied to news organizations that are planning to use AI anchors in a manner that would not compromise the credibility and trust of their audience.

item.title: The Roles of Source Citations in Identifying Misinformation and Disinformation: Moderating Effects of Digital Literacy and Information Types
item.dc:creator: Kyungwoo Kim, Seungheon Han, Sung‐Bou Kim, Ha Hwang
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Kyungwoo Kim, Seungheon Han, Sung‐Bou Kim, Ha Hwang

Topics: Misinformation, Disinformation, Digital literacy, Information credibility

This study investigates whether source citations enhance detection of false information and whether their effects depend on digital literacy and information processing style. In an experimental survey of 1,013 South Koreans, citations show no overall effect. However, they significantly improve detection of disinformation—but not misinformation—among individuals with higher digital literacy. Intuitive processing lowers detection ability, and citations do not counteract this tendency. The findings challenge assumptions that transparency universally improves evaluation, showing that citation effectiveness depends on user capabilities and the type of falsehood, and highlighting the need to strengthen digital literacy alongside transparency initiatives.

item.title: Selective appropriation and ideological framing in BBC Persian’s coverage of the Palestinian-Israeli conflict
item.dc:creator: Hamed Jokar Dehmorghouei, Mahmoud Afrouz, Akbar Hesabi
item.description:
Journalism · Hamed Jokar Dehmorghouei, Mahmoud Afrouz, Akbar Hesabi

Topics: Journalism studies, Media framing, News coverage, Political polarization

Drawing on narrative theory and the concept of “selective appropriation,” this research conducts a critical analysis of the translation practices of BBC Persian. The study analyzed the coverage of the Palestinian-Israeli conflict after the attacks of October 7, 2023. A corpus of 48 news reports originally published in English on the BBC World News website and their corresponding Persian translations were comparatively examined. The focus of the study was on the systematic use of omission, addition, substitution, and permutation strategies in the Persian translations of BBC Persian and their ideological implications. The findings demonstrated that BBC Persian engaged in narrative reframing. Throughout a sum of 198 main framing interventions, the Persian versions of the news reports were reframed to align with the presumed ideological and political sensitivities of the Persian-speaking audience. Main strategies consisted of the omission of designating Hamas as a terrorist organization and the addition of a broader geopolitical context. In addition to that, the substitution of claims with facts to assign culpability, and the permutation of the news body and headlines to shift narrative focus from human tragedy to state failure were used. The result was a “localized version” of the news reports that construct a different narrative and ideologically distinct reality from the English source texts.

item.title: News recommendation as a process: An interdisciplinary literature review
item.dc:creator: Laura Linda Laugwitz
item.description:
Journalism · Laura Linda Laugwitz

Topics: News recommendation, Communication science, Journalism, Communication theory

This paper investigates how different disciplines conceptualize news recommendation, addressing the challenge of fragmented knowledge in this interdisciplinary field. Through a comprehensive literature review of 476 peer-reviewed publications from 2000 to 2022, the study analyzes terminology, citation practices, and mental models in mainly computer science, communication science, and interdisciplinary research. We find distinct disciplinary terminologies and asymmetries in epistemic authority, with computer science dominating in publication volume and citations. The study identifies four mental models structuring researchers’ representations of news recommendation, ranging from system-centric technical optimization to abstract reflections on journalism. It proposes an interdisciplinary process model integrating technical and social dimensions to bridge knowledge silos and foster interdisciplinary collaboration. The paper concludes with strategies for researchers to promote interdisciplinarity, including learning other disciplinary languages and addressing power dynamics.

item.title: Producer, interrupted: The hidden toll of being a Global South producer making documentaries for the West
item.dc:creator: Saad Zuberi
item.description:
Journalism · Saad Zuberi

Topics: Journalism studies, Digital journalism, Media representation, Journalistic practice

Transnational documentary production relies heavily on Global South producers whose labor, expertise, and local knowledge remain central to nonfiction storytelling,yet their experiences and burdens often remain overlooked within scholarship on global journalism and representation. Drawing on dependency theory, postcolonial scholarship, and affective epistemology, I foreground documentary production as a critical site where power, authority, and authorship are negotiated. This allows me to examine how labor hierarchies and material inequalities shape both production and local producers’ embodied experiences. Using in-depth interviews with nine Pakistani producers alongside autoethnographic reflections from my own experience in transnational documentary production, I show how power asymmetries marginalize local producers despite their central creative and interpretive role. The findings identify an interconnected triple burden of material, narrative, and affective dependency at play. Local producers remain dependent not only on foreign funding and distribution infrastructures, but also on Western narrative frameworks that constrain which stories are funded, legitimized, and circulated globally. These asymmetries generate affective dependency, producing moral injury among local producers navigating unequal systems of representation.

item.title: The Trouble With Catching Up: Problematizing the “AI Gap” and its Global Inequities in Journalism
item.dc:creator: Nadja Schaetz, Anna Schjøtt
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Nadja Schaetz, Anna Schjøtt

Topics: Artificial intelligence in journalism, Digital divide, Journalism studies, Digital transformation

The “artificial intelligence (AI) gap” in journalism describes a divide between newsrooms equipped to innovate and benefit from AI and those left behind. Rather than an objective condition, this study examines this gap as a discursive construction, drawing on articulation theory. Using the JournalismAI Academy for Small Newsrooms as a case study, we combine ethnographic observation with interviews conducted in 2022 to 2023 and 2025. Findings demonstrate how technological lag is articulated as a problem and AI investment as its solution, a linkage stabilized through assumptions of inevitable, linear technological progress—legitimizing particular ways of thinking about and acting on AI.

item.title: Contradicting Epistemic Inequalities: The Case of the Journalist Navina Sundaram
item.dc:creator: Christina Haritos, Margreth Lünenborg
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Christina Haritos, Margreth Lünenborg

Topics: Journalism, Epistemology, Gender representation, Journalistic practice

This contribution asks how social inequalities are perpetuated through colonial silences maintained through practices of knowledge production in journalism. Drawing on postcolonial scholarship, it examines how these silences have historically been challenged between the 1960s and 1980s. Based on documents from the personal files of Navina Sundaram, one of the first non-White journalists on West German television, it traces the practices of contradicting that challenge and uphold journalistic epistemology: contradicting visibility in editorial practices, contradicting through international networks, and denying belonging. Together, these practices show how debates on diversity in German journalism are rooted in historical struggles for epistemic justice.

item.title: From Exposure to Creation: Cultivating Narrative Ownership to Reduce Stigma
item.dc:creator: Xun Zhu
item.description:
Communication Research · Xun Zhu

Topics: Narrative persuasion, Attitude change, Psychological ownership, Stigma

Stories are powerful agents of attitude change, including attitudes toward stigmatized groups. However, existing theories have focused on narrative exposure, with limited attention to narrative creation. Creating a story involves simulating characters and events and expressing them through language, which may engage unique psychological processes. This research investigates how and why creating stories shapes stigma. In three experiments, participants wrote, imagined, or read a positive story about a stigmatized character. Study 1 showed that narrative creation, especially writing, increased psychological ownership, which predicted greater transportation and lower stigma. Study 2 replicated these findings using a different stigmatized group. Study 3 showed that psychological ownership continued to explain the effects of narrative creation above and beyond perceived agency. These findings extend theories of narrative persuasion by considering the effects of story creation on intergroup attitudes and introducing psychological ownership as a novel mechanism linking creation to narrative processing and outcomes.

item.title: Complicating crisis narratives: Civic embeddedness and relational trust in the Zambian news ecosystem
item.dc:creator: Eddy Borges-Rey, Annastazia Ng’ambi
item.description:
Journalism · Eddy Borges-Rey, Annastazia Ng’ambi

Topics: Journalism, Media trust, Community radio, Civic engagement

Much of the recent academic discourse suggests journalism is in crisis due to declining revenues, reduced public trust, and digital disruptions (D’Arma et al., 2025). Zambia, however, offers a distinctive case of a proliferating media sector, growing newspaper readership, and journalists who retain strong public esteem despite material precarity (Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung, 2022; MISA Zambia, 2020; Mwimbe, 2023). Drawing on interviews with journalists, media practitioners, educators, and local leadership across Lusaka and Muchinga Province, this article examines how journalism and public information circulate across uneven urban and rural infrastructures. Findings reveal that Zambian journalism is driven by civic commitment, strong public trust, and adaptive practices. Community radio remains a central civic platform in rural areas, whilst trusted local intermediaries help relay information where direct journalistic reach is weakened by infrastructural constraints. Digital migration has encouraged content hybridity and audience engagement, with bloggers and news outlets negotiating legitimacy and symbolic power. Despite financial and logistical challenges, investigative journalism is gaining traction, supported by public appetite for accountability. Print media retains cultural authority, especially in regions with limited internet access. The study therefore argues that Zambia complicates dominant crisis narratives by showing that civic commitment, relational trust, and hybrid adaptation can sustain journalism under precarious conditions, even where labour insecurity, structural legal vulnerabilities, and territorial exclusion persist.

item.title: Objectivity as a shield: Journalistic voice and the strategic use of quotation in Iranian newspapers
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Makki
item.description:
Journalism · Mohammad Makki

Topics: Journalistic practice, News production, Professional norms, Media systems

This paper identifies and analyses a distinctive journalistic practice in Iranian political news reporting, termed the “projecting voice”. This practice, observed in reports from both conservative ( Kayhan ) and reformist ( Etemaad ) newspapers, involves a near-complete absence of explicit authorial/journalist opinion, where the journalist functions primarily as a conduit for the quoted statements of high-status sources. Using a discourse-analytical approach, this study argues that the “projecting voice” is not simply passive reporting, but a strategic ritual of impersonality in service of “objective” reporting. This ritual serves as a risk-management device, allowing journalists to navigate institutional pressures while creating a veneer of objectivity. This might be due to political reasons and the sensitivity around political topics and leaders. The paper concludes that this practice challenges conventional Western models of journalistic objectivity and provides a crucial case study of how professional norms are adapted in authoritarian media environments.

item.title: Brand governance in the platform economy: From political to regulatory recognition
item.dc:creator: Marco Scalvini
item.description:
New Media & Society · Marco Scalvini

Topics: Platform governance, Social media, Persuasion, Political communication

This article reconceptualises corporate advocacy as brand governance, a techno-normative promotional practice that regulates the conditions of political visibility within networked publics. Drawing on a sociosemiotic analysis of global advocacy campaigns (2017–2022), the analysis identifies three strategies, Visionary (“Feeling the Other”), Sensitive (“Feeling for Others”) and Reflexive (“Feeling with Others”), each operating through distinct affective and narrative logics. The argument advances a distinction between political and regulatory recognition. Political recognition acknowledges claims in their structural and collective dimension; regulatory recognition extends legitimacy only to claims aligned with the promotional regime’s affective and reputational logic. The evidence suggests that brand governance operates predominantly in this regulatory mode, producing a conditional visibility that privileges individualised emotional appeals over structural political demands. This study focuses on US and Western European promotional cultures; comparative research across other regions remains a necessary next step.

item.title: Does alternative news media inform or misinform voters during election campaigns?
item.dc:creator: Atle Haugsgjerd, Rune Karlsen, Tine Ustad Figenschou, Karoline Andrea Ihlebæk, Toril Aalberg
item.description:
New Media & Society · Atle Haugsgjerd, Rune Karlsen, Tine Ustad Figenschou, Karoline Andrea Ihlebæk, Toril Aalberg

Topics: Alternative media, Political knowledge, Political misinformation, Election campaigns

A growing body of literature has studied the audiences and effects of alternative media use. We contribute by examining how such usage shapes political knowledge during election campaigns. Given their partisan orientation, lack of professional verification, and often provocative style, alternative media are found to produce and circulate misinformation, even as their users are often politically engaged, active news consumers. We ask whether alternative media inform rather than misinform citizens during election campaigns. Adopting a two-dimensional conception of political knowledge, we examine both surveillance knowledge and confidence in that knowledge – along with misinformation understood as the combination of the two. Utilizing individual-level panel data from Norway, our findings suggest that alternative news use is not associated with being better or worse informed, but with being more confident in one’s political knowledge. We discuss how these effects may differ in more polarized or lower-quality information environments.

item.title: “A feeling reporter, not a robotic reporter”: Empathy, emotions, resilience, and vicarious post-traumatic growth after mass shootings
item.dc:creator: Lisa Krantz
item.description:
Journalism · Lisa Krantz

Topics: Journalistic practice, Mental health, Professional norms, Journalism studies

This study seeks to understand the experiences of journalists reporting on mass shootings. It explores the roles of empathy and emotionality and asks if normalizing them in journalism practice can strengthen resilience and promote vicarious post-traumatic growth. Although empathy and displays of emotion are not yet embraced as journalistic norms such as objectivity, all participants spoke of the importance of empathy, particularly when covering mass shootings. Interviews with 23 journalists who reported on the mass shooting at Robb Elementary School in Uvalde, Texas provide insight into their experiences. Although some participants differed in their views of shared emotionality, empathy, resilience, and vicarious post-traumatic growth were evident.

item.title: Sizzling spring: the construction of seasons and seasonal transitions in Australian journalism
item.dc:creator: Lawrie Zion, Henrik Bødker, Mona Chatskin
item.description:
Journalism · Lawrie Zion, Henrik Bødker, Mona Chatskin

Topics: Climate change communication, Journalism, Science journalism, News coverage

While much of humanity can insulate itself from the full impact of seasonal weather patterns, seasons remain tools for living that frame important recurrent events and thus help structure rhythms of life and, for many, livelihoods. Journalism plays a significant role in maintaining seasons as meaningful frames around, amongst other things, sports events, nature, and leisure. Such coverage has been termed seasonal journalism: recurrent content that helps structure the year and, increasingly, our relationships to a shifting climate. As past experiences lose some of their predictive power, journalism is engaging in new ways to make sense of seasons and their transitions. This article examines how five Australian news publications constructed seasons in articles published in August and September in 2023 and 2024, as these months mark the transition from winter to spring. A key takeaway is that seasonal characteristics, anomalies, transitions, and forecasts are increasingly becoming news events in their own right, rather than merely forming a backdrop for other stories. At the same time, more conventional seasonal content (such as articles about flower shows or swooping magpies) continues to appear. But even in these stories, there are tensions between anticipation and disruption, and with that, explicit or implied attempts to make sense of climatic changes. The analysis is based on 206 articles and draws on journalism studies, environmental communication and the environmental humanities.

item.title: Beyond the degree: Entry criteria and the influence of journalism education in Nigerian news organizations’ hiring practices
item.dc:creator: Kemi Busari
item.description:
Journalism · Kemi Busari

Topics: Journalism education, Journalistic practice, Professional norms, Journalism studies

This study examines the criteria that Nigerian news organizations prioritize when hiring reporters and the role of journalism education in this process. Drawing on 21 interviews with newsroom editors and 70 job advertisements, the analysis distinguishes between core “ultimate criteria” shared across organizations and more flexible “adaptable criteria” that reflect organizational and individual editors’ priorities. Framed within boundary work and gatekeeping theories, the study examines how hiring serves as a central site for regulating entry into the profession and reinforcing professional norms and values. The findings highlight the persistent gap between journalism education and industry expectations and carry important implications for policy, particularly regarding proposals to mandate journalism degrees for employment. By offering insights from an understudied context, this research advances understanding of newsroom hiring practices, the negotiation of professional boundaries, and the alignment of journalism education with industry needs in Nigeria.

item.title: Humility in journalism: The epistemic virtue that allows journalists to learn from experiences of others
item.dc:creator: Gregory Perreault, Claudia Mellado
item.description:
Journalism · Gregory Perreault, Claudia Mellado

Topics: Journalism, Journalistic practice, Epistemology, Professional norms

Journalists have long been associated with a strong ego and the hubris necessary to share the news as “the way it is.” But overlooked, and perhaps more important, is the humility required by journalists to gather new knowledge in the first place. Through the lens of joy and journalistic epistemology, the present study explores interviews with 27 journalists in Chile and the United States in regards to their experiences with humility. Journalists broadly believed that their work could be done without humility, but that good journalism necessitated humility. The best journalists, across these national contexts, were considered to be those who were humble: which journalists defined as being willing to listen, to learn, to be corrected and to apologize for mistakes.

item.title: What Do We Mean by Transparency? Conceptualizing and Operationalizing Transparency in Communication
item.dc:creator: Wenjia Yan, Li Jiang, Yiqian Gao, Pingping Jia
item.description:
Communication Research · Wenjia Yan, Li Jiang, Yiqian Gao, Pingping Jia

Topics: Communication theory, Media transparency, Research methodology, Public opinion

By analyzing 164 articles from communication journals published between 2002 and 2024, this scoping review systematically investigates temporal trends, conceptualizations, and operationalizations of transparency research within communication studies. The analysis identifies three primary conceptual dimensions of transparency: (1) information, encompassing both visibility and interpretation; (2) relations, functioning as an intermediary between dialogue and power; (3) values and norms, reflecting the tensions between ethical ideals and institutional constraints. Operationalization of transparency has predominantly relied on informational measures, whereas relational and value-based dimensions remain comparatively underdeveloped. Increasing attention has been directed toward subjective stakeholder perceptions, emphasizing transparency as a dynamic and context-dependent construct. Overall, the findings indicate that transparency extends beyond a stable informational attribute to incorporate relational and normative functions, while its enactment remains fluid, contextually shaped, and susceptible to unintended consequences.

item.title: The governance of snarking: Anti-fandom as tiny publics
item.dc:creator: Jessica S. H. Martin, Claudia Harris Coveney
item.description:
New Media & Society · Jessica S. H. Martin, Claudia Harris Coveney

Topics: Online communities, Social identity, Digital ethnography, Social justice

This article examines online celebrity ‘snarking’ communities, otherwise known as anti-fandom spaces or even hate forums. Specifically, we provide an analysis of the governance of these groups and how they develop a collective morality through both articulations with the celebrities’ mediation and with the logics of social justice. Using data collected from a digital ethnography of two popular celebrity snark spaces, we employ Critical Discourse Analysis to track the particular discursive repertoires and vernaculars which characterise snark across multiple platforms. We argue that despite the perceived ‘incivility’ of these online spaces, discourses of care, justice and solidarity often emerge which complicate existing narratives of these groups. Though participation in snarking collectives is often explained in pathologising or individualising narratives of anti-fandom, we demonstrate some of the reflexive work that happens in these spaces which sometimes ignites sociological discussions and frustrations at inequalities. We therefore conceptualise snark through the lens of a ‘tiny public’ that identifies and explores broader race and class injustice in contemporary society. Here, the prevailing discourses about celebrity subjects ‘failing upwards’ betrays an anger at elites who do not suffer the same material consequences at times of crisis; though many of these frustrations are misdirected back at the celebrity subject and manifest in a collective desire to see repercussions for the individual celebrity, rather than collective action aimed at the structures that make this failure possible, visible and even lucrative.

item.title: The Dark Side of Flow: Passive Flow State, Metacognitive Bias, and Compulsive Use of Short-Form Videos
item.dc:creator: Na Wang, Long Ma, Chei Sian Lee
item.description:
Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking · Na Wang, Long Ma, Chei Sian Lee

Topics: Short-form video, Compulsive use, Flow, Social media use

This study examines why short-form videos (SFVs) in social media foster compulsive use by reconceptualizing flow in low-effort digital environments. While prior research has primarily highlighted flow's optimal facets, this study argues that in passive media contexts, flow may also embody maladaptive qualities. Drawing on dual-process theory, SFV engagement is conceptualized as predominantly driven by intuitive processing in System 1 (heuristic processing related), through which flow weakens self-control monitoring of System 2 (systematic processing related). To capture the underlying psychological mechanisms, flow is reconceptualized as a passive psychological state comprising both immersive and maladaptive dimensions (i.e., concentration, enjoyment, telepresence, heightened arousal, affective reliance, and loss of self-reflection). In addition, the desirability- and feasibility-related cues embedded in digital environments are examined as heuristic triggers of passive flow state, while overestimation of self-control is conceptualized as a critical mediator linking flow to compulsive use. Survey data from 842 SFV users were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. The findings revealed that overestimation of self-control emerges as the strongest driver of compulsive use, exceeding the total effect of flow. Flow is found to both directly impact compulsive SFV use and indirectly through increasing the overestimation of self-control. At the subdimensional level, flow's dimensions exert divergent effects, with concentration, telepresence, and affective reliance significantly intensifying compulsive use and/or overestimation of self-control. By integrating a dual-process perspective with a multidimensional conceptualization of flow, this study advances understanding of how passive flow state fosters metacognitive bias and compulsive engagement, offering theoretical and practical insights to promote more sustainable digital environments that support users' well-being.

item.title: Value-motivated use of generative AI among student journalists: Practices and risk management in college newsrooms
item.dc:creator: Bailey Vergara, Bingbing Zhang
item.description:
Journalism · Bailey Vergara, Bingbing Zhang

Topics: Generative AI, Journalism education, Journalistic practice, Professional norms

Generative AI (GenAI) has rapidly entered journalistic practice, prompting growing scholarly attention to future journalists, particularly journalism students, and their attitudes and beliefs about its use. However, little research has examined how student journalists working in college newsrooms actually use GenAI in practice, or how they navigate its associated risks while upholding journalistic values. To address this gap, we conducted interviews with 20 student journalists working in college newsrooms. Our findings show that student journalists engage in value-motivated uses of GenAI, while also approaching the technology with caution. They actively navigate ethical concerns related to accuracy, transparency, accountability, and professional autonomy, and develop strategies to manage the risks that GenAI introduces into journalistic work. Our findings offer important theoretical contributions to understanding value-motivated uses of GenAI and perceptions of its associated risks. Our findings also provide practical implications for journalism education by informing how student journalists who represent the next generation of professionals can be better prepared to navigate an AI-mediated news environment.

item.title: Pseudo-journalistic political communication: The Flemish far right and the appropriation of journalism for political communication ends
item.dc:creator: Maximilian Grönegräs, Yazan Badran, Benjamin De Cleen
item.description:
Journalism · Maximilian Grönegräs, Yazan Badran, Benjamin De Cleen

Topics: Political communication, Journalism, Far right, Hybrid media system

The borders between journalism and politics have become increasingly blurry within the hybrid media system in which older and newer media logics as well as media and political logics interact in complex ways. This article examines an underexplored aspect of this evolving landscape: the appropriation of journalism for political communication ends by political parties, a phenomenon we call ‘pseudo-journalistic political communication’. With the far right having emerged as a key player in this hybridization, we examine the Belgian Vlaams Belang’s (Flemish Interest, VB) pseudo-journalistic political communication through a multimodal textual analysis of the VB ‘talk show’ VBTV and the VB-produced but seemingly independent ‘news website’ V-NIEUWS. Building on Ekman and Widholm’s (2024a) work, our study focuses on the combination of political communication logics and journalistic logics across four dimensions: (1) transparency concerning partisanship; (2) platforms used for dissemination; (3) journalistic genres and roles; and (4) discourse about journalism. Our findings highlight the party’s aptitude in drawing on journalistic logics for political communication ends but also the difficulties it faces in navigating the tensions between journalistic and political logics, particularly in formats that are more profoundly pseudo-journalistic. The conclusion builds on the comparison of V-NIEUWS and VBTV to refine the conceptualization of pseudo-journalistic political communication as one specific articulation of journalism into political communication. We also situate this phenomenon within the broader landscape of the far right’s multi-faceted engagement with journalism.

item.title: Toward an inclusive model of journalism education: Exploring factors shaping the classroom experience of a visually impaired instructor
item.dc:creator: Ibrahim Helmy Emara
item.description:
Journalism · Ibrahim Helmy Emara

Topics: Journalism education, Disability, Inclusion, Attitude change

Diversity, equity, and inclusion of visually impaired educators remain underexplored, particularly in fields that are heavily visually oriented, such as media and journalism. Drawing on the perspectives of 24 sighted journalism students in Egypt, this study investigates the factors that shape the classroom experience of a blind instructor, focusing on the interplay between pedagogical practices, student engagement, and institutional support. Using data collected through electronic interviews, the research examines how these dynamics influence student perceptions of competence, collaboration, and inclusion, as well as their broader attitudes toward disability. Findings highlight the complex relational and institutional processes that contribute to effective inclusion. Students’ engagement, combined with adaptive teaching strategies and systemic support, facilitated an environment in which disability was decoupled from assumptions of incompetence, allowing professional capabilities to be foregrounded. The study situates these insights within the framework of critical disability studies, emphasizing the social and structural dimensions of inclusion rather than framing success as an individual achievement. By conceptualizing inclusive pedagogy as a dynamic, multi-stakeholder process, this research offers a model for integrating visually impaired educators in visually oriented disciplines and contributes to broader discussions on dismantling ableist norms and fostering equitable academic environments.

item.title: Infrastructures of listening: AI and the reconfiguration of community-centered newswork
item.dc:creator: Claire Wardle
item.description:
Journalism · Claire Wardle

Topics: Artificial intelligence in journalism, Journalistic practice, Audience engagement, Community engagement

This study examines how AI-supported tools can reshape journalistic epistemologies, labor practices, and community relationships through an in-depth qualitative analysis of “Listening Across Divides,” a collaborative project conducted by NPR in the lead-up to the 2024 U.S. election. Drawing on interviews with journalists, editors, and project staff across nine public media stations, the study explores how AI-mediated systems designed to record, organize, and surface themes from facilitated community conversations intersected with engagement-oriented journalism practices. Findings show that AI functioned less as a tool for automation than as an infrastructural layer supporting collective listening and cross-newsroom sense-making. The study demonstrates how technologies associated with efficiency and scale may simultaneously support and reshape slower forms of community-centered journalism rooted in sustained listening. In doing so, the article contributes to scholarship on engagement journalism, AI in newswork, and journalistic knowledge production by conceptualizing AI as a sociotechnical infrastructure for mediated collective sense-making.

item.title: Generative Logic and the Mediatization of Politics: Deepfake Parodies and Political Reinterpretation in China
item.dc:creator: Tianru Guan, 郭文蕙, Yilu Yang
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Tianru Guan, 郭文蕙, Yilu Yang

Topics: Mediatization of politics, Generative AI, Deepfakes, Political communication

This study revisits the theory of the mediatization of politics in the era of artificial intelligence (AI), questioning its applicability beyond Western democracies and proposing an extension through the concept of generative logic. Drawing on the analysis of AI-generated parodies in China’s cyberspace, it examines a distinctive mode of political communication in which foreign political figures’ faces are superimposed onto characters from Chinese historical television dramas. These satirical videos construct five patterns of analogical displacement, enabling users to reinterpret international affairs through culturally familiar frameworks. Rather than merely destabilizing truth boundaries, this content reflects a locally embedded form of AI-mediated political expression shaped by the interplay of political logic , media logic , and generative logic . We conceptualize this configuration as a multi-logic communicative structure that sustains a stable yet dynamic mode of political discourse in authoritarian contexts. The findings contribute to a broader understanding of how generative technologies reshape political engagement, symbolic meaning-making, and mediated reality across diverse political systems.

item.title: From Structural Inequalities to Labor Precarity: Adoption of Digital and AI Tools in Latin American Journalism
