item.dc:creator: Miguel Garcés-Prettel, Jesús Arroyave, Summer Harlow, Lilian Kanashiro, Mariana De Maio, Janara Nicoletti, Adriana Amado, Dasniel Olivera Pérez, Martín Oller Alonso, Celeste González de Bustamante
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Miguel Garcés-Prettel, Jesús Arroyave, Summer Harlow, Lilian Kanashiro, Mariana De Maio, Janara Nicoletti, Adriana Amado, Dasniel Olivera Pérez, Martín Oller Alonso, Celeste González de Bustamante

Topics: Digital journalism, Artificial intelligence in journalism, Digital divide, Journalism studies

While inequalities in technological access and use have been widely documented, few studies have examined their link to labor precarity and social inequality in journalism in the Global South. This article analyzes this relationship through a multilevel study of Worlds of Journalism Study data from 4,250 journalists in 11 Latin American countries. Results show that macro-level inequality, measured by the Gini coefficient, is not associated with the use of advanced digital technologies, including AI, while micro-level precarity, expressed in contractual instability and excessive workloads, is. Working conditions, rather than national disparities, are key to explaining inequalities in technology adoption.

item.title: Technology-Facilitated Sexual Violence and Abuse in Asian Societies: A Scoping Review
item.dc:creator: Gowoon Jung, Yongri Li, Gaeun Son
item.description:
Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking · Gowoon Jung, Yongri Li, Gaeun Son

Topics: Online harassment, Deepfakes, Mental health, Platform governance

Technology-facilitated sexual violence and abuse (TFSVA) has rapidly emerged as a pervasive form of gender-based violence in Asia, yet regionally grounded syntheses remain scarce. This scoping review systematically reviewed empirical studies on TFSVA in Asian societies, focusing on how cultural contexts and platform ecosystems shape victimization, coping, and governance. Using PRISMA-ScR-consistent procedures, 22 studies published between 2021 and 2025 were identified across databases and analyzed, with all included studies focusing on adult populations. Across studies, TFSVA appears as a continuum of overlapping harms, with image-based abuse and deepfakes generating persistent, networked exposure that extends into mental health distress, social withdrawal, and offline safety risks. Coping strategies are characterized by low-visibility, individualized risk management shaped by stigma and institutional uncertainty, while culture and infrastructure jointly shape harm recognition and help-seeking. The review highlights the need for comparative, platform- and governance-focused research that integrates mental health outcomes and cultural context.

item.title: The institutional logic of news source selection in clentelistic media systems: A comparative study of Albania and Kosovo
item.dc:creator: Lindita Camaj, Alban Tartari, Dren Gërguri
item.description:
Journalism · Lindita Camaj, Alban Tartari, Dren Gërguri

Topics: News sourcing, Media systems, Journalistic practice, Political communication

This study examines source diversity in broadcast news in Albania and Kosovo’s hybrid clientelist media systems. Drawing on institutional theory, we explore how sourcing practices reflect competing logics of power, professionalism, and market pressures under conditions of uncertainty. Using a mixed-method approach that combines content analysis of prime-time news with survey data from journalists, we assess both the visibility of political and societal actors and the factors shaping source selection. Findings reveal persistent elite-centric sourcing patterns, with significant variation between the two countries. Albanian journalists report stronger influence from media owners, managers, and government institutions, indicating a highly hierarchical and clientelist structure. In contrast, Kosovo’s media system exhibits a more fragmented and fluid environment. Theoretically, this research challenges assumptions that institutionalized routines uniformly produce news source homogeneity or that clientelist systems completely suppress pluralism. By situating source diversity as a proxy for power distribution, the study contributes to debates on journalism in transitional democracies and highlights the tension between normative ideals and the realities of hybrid clientelistic media systems.

item.title: How structural and cultural violence shape journalists’ experiences and coping strategies: An intersectional analysis
item.dc:creator: Clémence Petit
item.description:
Journalism · Clémence Petit

Topics: Journalism, Journalistic practice, Professional identity, Well-being

While many studies have focused on direct and external attacks threatening journalists’ safety, this article examines how journalists experience and cope with structural and cultural violence emanating from within the journalistic field itself. This study analyzes 33 in-depth interviews with a diverse sample of journalists in French-speaking Belgium – including freelancers, journalists without press cards, and minority journalists. The analysis reveals how intersecting identity markers (gender, race, age), organizational factors (employment status, beat), and newsroom culture shape journalists’ experiences of three forms of structural violence: discrimination, trauma exposure, and economic precarity. Discrimination experienced by minority journalists elicits primarily resilience strategies; trauma exposure associated with certain beats leads to emotional withdrawal and mental health conditions; while economic violence, particularly acute among freelancers, results mostly in compliance and avoidance strategies, which can result in burn-out or exit from the profession. Crucially, cultural violence emerges as normalizing these harms by dismissing microaggressions, framing trauma as inevitable, and presenting precarity as vocational sacrifice. The study reveals that journalists face these difficulties largely in isolation, with individual coping strategies proving exhausting and unsustainable over time, highlighting the need for institutional support.

item.title: Posting under pressure: Politicians active on social media are more stressed
item.dc:creator: Majbritt Kappelgaard Severin‐Nielsen
item.description:
New Media & Society · Majbritt Kappelgaard Severin‐Nielsen

Topics: Social media use, Political communication, Mental health, Online harassment

While social media has become an indispensable tool for politicians’ communication with citizens and other stakeholders, emerging qualitative evidence suggests that its use may be associated with diminished well-being and reduced performance within the parliamentary arena – potentially undermining democratic processes. Combining insights from a representative survey study of politicians in Denmark ( n = 1233) with data on their observed social media usage (Facebook: 24,625 posts; Instagram: 13,019 posts), this study is the first to test the generalizability of this emerging evidence and advance our theoretical understanding of the conditions under which politicians’ social media usage is connected to stress. The study demonstrates a significant, positive correlation between politicians’ social media usage and self-reported stress symptoms and points to excessive usage as the primary explanation behind the association. Furthermore, exposure to online harassment is a crucial mediating factor in the association.

item.title: A scoping review of anglophone scholarship on trauma and journalism in sub-Saharan Africa
item.dc:creator: Emma Heywood, Margaret R. Grundy, Elana Newman
item.description:
Journalism · Emma Heywood, Margaret R. Grundy, Elana Newman

Topics: Journalism studies, Trauma, Journalist safety, Media coverage

This scoping review maps anglophone scholarship on trauma and journalism in and/or about sub-Saharan Africa published between 1990 and 2025. Rather than assuming a single universal definition of trauma, the review examines how trauma is implicitly and explicitly conceptualised within this literature. Drawing on 139 peer-reviewed journal articles identified through searches of four academic databases, the review analyses patterns in trauma type, methodology, country focus, authorship location, and media platform. The findings indicate that trauma is conceptualised inconsistently across the literature, with only 28% of studies explicitly employing the term. Trauma coverage nevertheless closely mirrors regional crisis contexts. Conflict and war dominate studies focused on Nigeria, Sudan, South Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo, and Somalia, while political and societal trauma cluster around election-related violence in Kenya, Nigeria, and Zimbabwe. Violence and crime, particularly gender-based violence, are most prominent in South African scholarship. Since 2010, journalist safety has emerged as a growing area of concern, particularly in Zimbabwe, Nigeria, and South Africa, while health-related trauma remains comparatively marginal despite the continent’s significant disease burden. Qualitative methods dominate the reviewed literature, while quantitative and mixed-methods research remain limited. Patterns of authorship further suggest differences in knowledge production in which Africa-based scholars more frequently produce locally grounded qualitative research, while non-Africa-based scholars disproportionately publish conceptual or theoretical work. The review identifies important conceptual, geographic, and methodological gaps and argues for more contextually grounded and trauma-informed approaches to journalism research relating to sub-Saharan Africa.

item.title: China’s mediated public diplomacy on climate change: Cross-media dynamics between Chinese, US, and UK news outlets
item.dc:creator: Wodong Guo, Zhong Zhang
item.description:
Journalism · Wodong Guo, Zhong Zhang

Topics: Public diplomacy, Climate change communication, Media coverage, Cross-cultural communication

This research investigates China’s mediated public diplomacy on climate change in the context of China’s “Media Going Global” campaign and its pursuit for leadership in global climate governance. Utilizing mixed computational analyses on a 6-year news corpus (2020-2025), this study examines the potential of China’s outward news channels shaping the salience of China-related climate issues in American and British media. It finds that, while China succeeds in ensuring its climate commitments acknowledged in foreign coverage, foreign evaluations of its climate actions remain largely independent of its mediated messaging. This article underscores the significance of considering the nature of issue when examining mediated public diplomacy. Climate change, unlike more contentious political issues, enables some alignments between China and western media through shared acknowledgment of climate crisis and China’s pivotal role, but remains limited to swing China’s climate image.

item.title: Algorithmic imaginaries: Definition and critical questions
item.dc:creator: Andreas Schellewald, Ellenrose Firth, Hui Lin
item.description:
New Media & Society · Andreas Schellewald, Ellenrose Firth, Hui Lin

Topics: Algorithmic curation, Human-computer interaction, Artificial intelligence, Algorithmic literacy

Algorithmic systems play an increasingly central role across a variety of social domains. Over the last few years, various concepts have been developed in the interdisciplinary field of algorithm studies to understand how people make sense of these systems and interact with them – including mental models of algorithms, folk theories of algorithms, or algorithmic imaginaries. This theoretical article engages with the concept of the algorithmic imaginary in particular. It argues that the concept of the algorithmic imaginary occupies a unique position in literature, foregrounding questions of affect and emotion in human-algorithm interaction, and theorising the dynamics of sense-making about algorithms in such terms. Critically examining work that has explicitly applied and developed the concept, we synthesise the scholarship, offer an updated definition, and pose critical questions for future research, including on emergent artificial intelligence phenomena.

item.title: Rendering the whole world blank: Precarity, totalising fear and digital scrolling
item.dc:creator: Alex Paterson
item.description:
New Media & Society · Alex Paterson

Topics: Digital media, Well-being, Mental health, Social media use

This article explores the connection between structurally induced precarity and the material practice of digital scrolling in the global north. It argues in favour of an expanded definition of precarity and that precarity, as a generalised affective condition, results in a state of totalising fear (fear which relates, at once, to discrete objects as well as the world itself). In that context, this article advances the claim that scrolling can be understood as an affective attachment (of the kind outlined by Lauren Berlant), developed in response to totalising fear, and which enables the subject to suspend time and to escape from conscious experience of precarity. In establishing this conclusion, the article also explores how the form of scrolling engenders an absorbing, passive and essentially ‘blank’ experience of the world, and how the attainment of this state is an expression of a limited, precarious mode of agency.

item.title: Silent yet Not Deserted: Associations Between Ringer Modes, Mobile Phone Use, and Digital Stress
item.dc:creator: Lise-Marie Nassen, Kathrin Karsay
item.description:
Mobile Media & Communication · Lise-Marie Nassen, Kathrin Karsay

Topics: Smartphone use, Digital stress, Digital well-being, Smartphone regulation

While digital disconnection and smartphone regulation have gained scholarly attention, little is known about phone setting customizations. Currently, there is inconsistent evidence on whether modifying ringer modes reduces actual smartphone use and digital stress. Some studies suggest that a silent mode can reduce phone attentiveness, whereas others deem it ineffective or counterproductive. Drawing on self-determination theory, we explore the associations between preferred ringer mode, smartphone use (i.e., screen time and number of unlocks), and digital stress, alongside intrinsic and extrinsic motivations. We analyzed data from a quota-based survey of 386 smartphone users in Flanders (Belgium) using structural equation modeling multigroup analyses. Our study revealed few direct associations between preferred ringer mode and smartphone use or digital stress. However, our findings underscore the crucial role of motivation in choosing a ringer mode, revealing multiple significant associations among intrinsic and extrinsic motivations, phone use, and digital stress. We discuss these theoretical and empirical findings in light of self-determination theory.

item.title: Mobile AI Service Robots and Everyday Politics of Space
item.dc:creator: Chris Chesher, Justine Humphry
item.description:
Mobile Media & Communication · Chris Chesher, Justine Humphry

Topics: Artificial intelligence, Mobile media, Platform governance, Digital labor

This article examines the rise of a new generation of mobile service robots that use AI for navigation and communication in public and semipublic spaces. Reviewing the state of the field of service robots and robot scholarship, this paper is a literature-informed commentary on mobile AI service robots as mobile media and their implications for human workers and the public, shared environments, and regulation in everyday spaces. We examine how mobile AI service robots are increasingly appearing in restaurants, hotels, university campuses, and public streets as service workers, tools, and social actors, introducing new modalities of communication, and reshaping spatial relationships, labour practices and power dynamics. These developments raise critical questions about the effect of robots’ communicative acts of movement, interfacing and emotional expression on others, the organisation of labour, and their role in the privatisation and surveillance of space. Ultimately, we argue that as mobile AI becomes embedded in ordinary life and work settings, it necessitates a renewed focus on who benefits, who is displaced, and how these increasingly agentic actors are governed as they become normalised in shared and public spaces.

item.title: The intermedia influence of X on legacy media coverage of the 2023 harmonised elections in Zimbabwe
item.dc:creator: Lungile Augustine Tshuma, Siphathisiwe M Ndlovu
item.description:
Journalism · Lungile Augustine Tshuma, Siphathisiwe M Ndlovu

Topics: Agenda-setting, Social media, News coverage, Political communication

The legacy media has for many years been instrumental and central in setting news agenda. In Africa, where the majority of the population dwells in rural areas, the centrality of the legacy media in setting news agenda is not in doubt. However, digital platforms have of late been key platforms for news resulting in them competing with the legacy media in setting news agenda. The purpose of this paper is to examine the intermedia relationship between X and legacy media in Zimbabwe within the theoretical framework of agenda-setting. The study sought to find out the intermedia agenda setting between X and the legacy media in Zimbabwe, namely, NewsDay and The Herald . The two publications represent the polarised Zimbabwe media system and the broader socio economic and political landscape. For analysis, Rozelli Campbell’s intermedia agenda cross-lagged correlation method was used. Findings demonstrate that X influenced legacy media’s reportage on elections during the given period. However, there were strong correlations between X and NewsDay as compared to The Herald .

item.title: Care, competence, or control? The evolution of parental supervision tools on social media platforms: A cross-platform comparison
item.dc:creator: Amanda Cipriani, Tama Bruno Leaver, Michele Willson
item.description:
New Media & Society · Amanda Cipriani, Tama Bruno Leaver, Michele Willson

Topics: Parental mediation, Platform governance, Social media platforms, Platform affordances

Interaction with social media constitutes a significant part of children’s online experiences, with the potential for both positive and negative experiences. Social media platforms provide parental “supervision tools” as a mechanism for balancing children’s autonomy with safeguards, promoting this function to parents to ensure safer digital practices for their children. This research adopts a constructivist framework to investigate the evolution and operationalisation of parental supervision across Instagram, Snapchat, and TikTok. Utilising qualitative methodology, this study combines archival data from an ethnographic walkthrough conducted in 2024, simulating a child’s and parent’s account for each platform. The cross-platform comparison reveals how platforms construct parental responsibility through their discursive and interface supervision mechanisms, expressed through macro-narratives, meso-contexts, and micro-practices. In doing so, platforms shift responsibility for regulation to parents as the accountable supervisory actors, while ultimately also controlling the supervision practices of these parents through the affordances and constraints offered through supervision tools.

item.title: Awe, Attention, and the Psychology of Perception
item.dc:creator: Brenda K. Wiederhold
item.description:
Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking · Brenda K. Wiederhold

Topics: Media psychology, Attention, Information processing, Well-being

item.title: Maintaining place: How journalists preserve their communities during times of dislocation
item.dc:creator: Tyler W. S. Nagel, Scott A. Eldridge, Marcel Broersma
item.description:
Journalism · Tyler W. S. Nagel, Scott A. Eldridge, Marcel Broersma

Topics: Journalistic practice, Crisis communication, Social identity, Digital displacement

During the 2023 wildfires in Canada’s Northwest Territories, journalists evacuated alongside residents. Spread across Canada, they continued to report on and for a community that had been dislocated. This paper argues that, in such conditions, local journalism adopts a place maintenance function, preserving and repairing a shared sense of “home” when physical proximity is no longer possible. Building on concepts of imagined communities, place maintenance, and interpretive communities, we show Northern journalists sustain continuity through three mechanisms. First, they reaffirm a distinct Northern identity and its boundaries. Second, they coordinate and legitimate shared interpretations of the crisis within a small Northern journalistic community. Third, they enact custodial relationships with audiences through translation, coordination, and information provision when routine infrastructures falter. Across these practices, coverage is oriented toward restoring the status quo ante , clarifying journalism’s continuity work and the conditions under which place maintenance takes place during periods of rupture.

item.title: Public Self-Consciousness and Anticipatory Avatar Customization in Korean Metaverse Platform
item.dc:creator: Upyong Hong, Hyenyeong Chung, Yunju Nam
item.description:
Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking · Upyong Hong, Hyenyeong Chung, Yunju Nam

Topics: Virtual reality, Self-presentation, Social identity, Cross-cultural communication

This study examines how public self-consciousness influences anticipatory avatar customization in Korean metaverse platform environments. In Study 1, 50 Korean university students created avatars under four conditions using iFland: free creation, private context, public context, and actual-self representation. Study 2 involved 100 independent raters evaluating the public suitability of freely created avatars. Results revealed that 96 percent created avatars differing from their actual appearance. Counterintuitively, individuals with higher public self-consciousness and agreeableness were significantly less likely to modify avatars for public contexts ( p < 0.05). Study 2 confirmed that unmodified avatars were rated more suitable for public contexts ( p < 0.05), suggesting that socially conscious individuals proactively incorporated appropriateness into initial designs. These preliminary findings suggest that Korean university students’ cultural emphasis on social harmony may shape virtual identity through anticipatory rather than reactive customization, though cross-cultural replication with diverse samples is needed to establish the generalizability of these patterns.

item.title: Trust beyond algorithms: What drives Italian audiences’ perceptions of search results and news produced with AI
item.dc:creator: Giulia Sbaraini Fontes, Sergio Splendore
item.description:
European Journal of Communication · Giulia Sbaraini Fontes, Sergio Splendore

Topics: Artificial intelligence in journalism, Media trust, Generative AI, Algorithmic curation

This article examines what drives audiences’ trust levels across different configurations of artificial intelligence (AI) use within the information ecosystem. We rely on a representative survey of Italian adults, performed in September 2025, to analyse trust patterns when (a) AI acts as an intermediary through automated search results and (b) when it is embedded in news organisations. Our findings show that AI-generated search results are more trusted than news, highlighting the growing role of platforms as primary information providers. Moreover, trust in news is positively associated with trust in news produced with AI, regardless of the source, challenging prevailing assumptions of ‘algorithmic aversion’ even in a traditional setting like Italy. These results suggest a shift in the foundations of media trust, with important implications for the role of journalism in an increasingly platform-driven information ecosystem.

item.title: Online Social Anxiety in the Digital Age: Transitions, Predictors, and Mental Health Associations in Emerging Adulthood
item.dc:creator: Ao Liu, Zheng Zhang, Xintian Hong, Rumiao Pan, Zhihao Ma, Yuanyuan Wang
item.description:
Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking · Ao Liu, Zheng Zhang, Xintian Hong, Rumiao Pan, Zhihao Ma, Yuanyuan Wang

Topics: Online social anxiety, Emerging adulthood, Latent transition analysis, Mental health

BACKGROUND: Online social anxiety (OSA), a multidimensional form of social evaluative anxiety in online social contexts, disproportionately affects emerging adults who constitute the largest active group of media users and face heightened psychological sensitivity due to growing pressures and immature sociocognitive regulation during the transition to adulthood. However, its heterogeneity, transitions, and longitudinal associations with mental health outcomes remain underexplored. METHODS: = 21.6 years; 50.4 percent female) assessed at 4-month intervals. Individuals were classified using latent profile analysis and the stability and changes of profiles were assessed via latent transition analysis (LTA). Multinomial logistic regressions were conducted separately at baseline and follow-up to identify correlates of profile membership. Predictors of profile transitions were examined using manual three-step LTA models, and associations between latent transition patterns and follow-up mental health outcomes were examined using BCH-LTA distal outcome analyses controlling for the corresponding baseline symptom level. RESULTS: Four profiles of OSA were identified: low, privacy-sensitive, moderate-high, and high OSA. Extreme profiles (low/high OSA) showed high stability (80.4 percent and 79.1 percent), while privacy-sensitive OSA exhibited the lowest stability (55.1 percent). Profile memberships were influenced by social-cognitive biases and digital interaction, particularly fear of negative evaluation and online interpersonal trust, whereas profile transitions were mainly associated with anxiety. Transitions toward less severe OSA profiles were generally associated with better subsequent mental health, whereas transitions toward more severe profiles corresponded to poorer outcomes, particularly for offline social anxiety. CONCLUSION: OSA was heterogeneous in its manifestation, severity and transitions. Personalized and early interventions targeting profile-specific vulnerabilities are critical to prevent the worsening of OSA and mitigate its psychological burden.

item.title: Playing with Fire, Losing the Drive: Bidirectional Links Between Problematic Smartphone Use and Grit Dimensions
item.dc:creator: Luming Zhao, Jiaxi Peng
item.description:
Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking · Luming Zhao, Jiaxi Peng

Topics: Problematic smartphone use, Smartphone use, Cognitive flexibility, Longitudinal study

This study examined bidirectional longitudinal associations between grit dimensions (consistency of interest [CI] and perseverance of effort [PE]) and problematic smartphone use (PSU) and tested cognitive flexibility as a mediating mechanism. A sample of 1,641 Chinese university students (55.2 percent female; Mage = 20.1 years) completed measures at two time points 6 months apart. A four-variable cross-lagged panel model revealed that CI and PSU negatively predicted each other over time, whereas PSU unidirectionally predicted decreased PE. Cognitive flexibility partially mediated the PSU-to-PE pathway (indirect effect = -0.004, 95 percent bootstrap CI [-0.010, -0.0001]). Competing models analysis confirmed this directionality: the forward mediation (PSU → cognitive flexibility → PE) was significant, whereas the reverse was not. These findings demonstrate that grit dimensions exhibit distinct longitudinal patterns with PSU and identify cognitive flexibility as a cognitive mechanism through which PSU specifically undermines effort persistence. Implications for dimensional approaches to grit and targeted interventions are discussed.

item.title: The Hollowing Out of Nonprofit News: An Ethnographic Investigation into the Implications of Exploited News Workers
item.dc:creator: Jocelyn McKinnon-Crowley
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Jocelyn McKinnon-Crowley

Topics: News organizations, Digital labor, Journalistic practice, Journalism studies

This work examines the practices of news workers within the unique funding structures of nonprofit news organizations using qualitative interviews and ethnographic methods. From a political economy perspective, my findings show that organizational concerns are prioritized over journalism by news workers in nonprofit news contexts. I argue this exploits public-service oriented journalists to do unpaid labor. I suggest that dependence on external funders reduces the power of nonprofit news organizations to do journalism.

item.title: Algorithmic muteness: How algorithmic management obstructs platform content operators’ resonance with their labor
item.dc:creator: Zhenyu Qiu, Jinfeng Du, Irina Y. Yu, Jiankun Gong, Yu Zuo
item.description:
New Media & Society · Zhenyu Qiu, Jinfeng Du, Irina Y. Yu, Jiankun Gong, Yu Zuo

Topics: Algorithmic curation, Platform labor, Social media algorithms, Digital labor

Workers who plan, curate, and promote content fuel platforms’ traffic success, yet frequently experience their labor as leaving no meaningful trace. While critical scholarship links this estrangement to algorithmic management, how it reshapes the quality of workers’ relationship with their own labor remains underexplored. Drawing on Rosa’s Resonance Theory and 27 interviews with platform content operators at China’s leading internet companies, this study reveals how algorithmic management obstructs resonance across content production, distribution, and feedback. Quantification hollows out labor’s normative worth; black-boxing forecloses self-efficacy through the (un)controllability paradox; amplification and acceleration suspend the possibility of self-transformation, even amid measurable success. We conceptualize ‘algorithmic muteness’, which captures a relational state—workers maintain high-intensity, data-mediated contact with their labor, yet this contact rarely yields genuine responsiveness. Algorithmic muteness moves beyond documenting the static, structural consequences of algorithmic management (e.g. alienation, meaninglessness) to tracing the relational process producing them, while critically revealing algorithms’ deep entanglement with platform capital.

item.title: Twitter Conversations: Gendered Issue Publics Among Women
item.dc:creator: Caley Hewitt, Ayla Oden, Nichole M. Bauer
item.description:
Communication Research · Caley Hewitt, Ayla Oden, Nichole M. Bauer

Topics: Gender differences, Twitter, Issue publics, Political discussion

We investigate how gender shapes women’s political discussion on Twitter using an issue publics framework. We test whether the conditions for gendered issue publics to form among women around feminine issues exist using data on political discussion via social media in the 2020 and 2022 elections. Our data includes political discussion among political candidates, elites, and non-elites, or regular people. Our results reveal several key findings. First, we find that men elites were more likely to discuss feminine issues, such as health care, compared to women elites, but we found no gender differences between regular Twitter users in our sample. Democratic women elites are more likely to discuss equity-based feminine issues, such as equal pay, than Republican women elites, but we find no partisan differences among non-elite women. We also find no gender or partisan differences at the elite and non-elite levels in the discussion of trait-based feminine issues, such as education. Finally, we show that in 2022, the Dobbs decision that rescinded the constitutional right to an abortion in the U.S. increased the salience of this issue among both women and men. Overall, our research suggests that the conditions for issue publics among women may not strongly exist as we find that non-elite men talk about feminine issues too.

item.title: The role of AI competencies: How do AI knowledge, skills, and attitudes shape users’ understanding and evaluation of explainable news recommendations?
item.dc:creator: Chuanji Wang, Anne C. Kroon, Judith E. Möller, Claes H. de Vreese, Sophie C. Boerman
item.description:
New Media & Society · Chuanji Wang, Anne C. Kroon, Judith E. Möller, Claes H. de Vreese, Sophie C. Boerman

Topics: Artificial intelligence, Algorithmic curation, News media, Trust

This study investigates how explanations in AI-driven news recommender systems (RS) influence user understanding, trust, and attitudes toward the RS, and whether these effects depend on individual differences in AI competence. An online experiment ( N = 754) was conducted in the Netherlands with a no-explanation condition as baseline. Results show that joint explanations significantly improved users’ objective understanding of the RS but had no consistent direct effects on perceived understanding, trust, or attitudes toward the RS. Exploratory structural equation modeling revealed an indirect pathway in which explanations enhanced objective understanding, which increased perceived understanding, subsequently fostering greater trust and more positive attitudes. Moderation analyses showed limited evidence for AI competence conditioning explanation effects, with small benefits concentrated among users with higher AI knowledge. Together, these findings suggest that explanations in news RS are not universally effective: their effects appear to operate primarily through cognitive mechanisms, while competence-related differences remain limited and selective.

item.title: The Meanings of News: How U.S. Adults Think About the Word “News”
item.dc:creator: Stephanie Edgerly, Ayse D. Lokmanoglu, Christopher M. Dobmeier, Nathan Walter
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Stephanie Edgerly, Ayse D. Lokmanoglu, Christopher M. Dobmeier, Nathan Walter

Topics: News consumption, Journalism studies, Communication theory, Political communication

This study explores the immediate, top-of-mind meanings audiences hold about “news.” Inspired by recent audience-centric approaches in defining news, we adopt a schema framework to investigate mental representations of the news concept. Using a national probability survey of U.S. adults, we employ a thought-listing exercise combined with a network analysis. Our findings paint a complex picture of news and its meaning today. We identify six distinct news schemas (i.e., clusters of co-occurring words) that correspond to different audience demographics, political ideology, and news consumption. The findings underscore that news is a dynamic concept with implications for journalism scholarship and practice.

item.title: Do WhatsApp news channels help users navigate the information environment? A field experiment on information-related attitudes
item.dc:creator: Camila Mont’Alverne, Patrícia Rossini, Antonis Kalogeropoulos
item.description:
New Media & Society · Camila Mont’Alverne, Patrícia Rossini, Antonis Kalogeropoulos

Topics: WhatsApp, Misinformation, Media trust, News fatigue

Messaging applications have become central sources of news, especially in the Global South, raising concerns about the quality of information circulating in these spaces. This study examines how receiving news through WhatsApp channels shapes key information-related attitudes in Brazil, including misinformation belief, news fatigue, and media trust. In a pre‑registered experiment conducted in November/December 2024, 601 participants from multiple Brazilian states were asked to subscribe to either a regional news channel or a fact‑checking channel operated by Globo, the largest media group in Latin America. The results show that accessing news via WhatsApp does not alter more stable attitudes, such as belief in misinformation or trust. However, it does reduce news fatigue and increases engagement with news on WhatsApp. As news consumption shifts toward private messaging platforms, these findings suggest their value lies less in reshaping political attitudes and more in maintaining routine connections between audiences and journalism.

item.title: Presumed media influence and support for social media bans: The roles of social and elite-based validation
item.dc:creator: Sarah Geber, Anne Markham Schulz, Mike Steffen Schäfer, Thomas N. Friemel
item.description:
New Media & Society · Sarah Geber, Anne Markham Schulz, Mike Steffen Schäfer, Thomas N. Friemel

Topics: Presumed media influence, Social media, Public opinion, Social norms

The study examines how presumed influences of social media on young people, as well as perceptions of how widely such beliefs are shared, shape support for social media bans. Extending the Influence of Presumed Influence (IPI) model, we introduce second-order presumed influences, defined as perceptions about how widely others presume media influences, and propose a mechanism of social validation. We additionally examine elite-based validation, referring to perceived beliefs of influential actors (i.e. scientists, politicians, and the media), as well as perceived social norms. Using survey data ( N = 1270) collected in the context of debates about a social media ban for minors under 16 in Switzerland, we find that stronger presumed influences predict support for a ban. While we find no support for social validation, the results point to the relevance of elite-related perceptions, particularly presumed scientific consensus. Perceived social norms of ban support emerge as an additional predictor of regulatory preferences.

item.title: A Viral War: Threat Perceptions in Light of Social Media News Consumption on the Russo-Ukrainian War
item.dc:creator: Tamás Tóth, Phelia Weiß, Kevin Koban, Ines Katrin Spielvogel, Jörg Matthes
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Tamás Tóth, Phelia Weiß, Kevin Koban, Ines Katrin Spielvogel, Jörg Matthes

Topics: Cultivation theory, Social media news, Threat perception, Russo-Ukrainian War

This article explores how social media news on the Russo-Ukrainian War shapes people’s perceptions of security through the lens of cultivation theory. Drawing on focus groups ( N = 31), Study 1 shows that Austrian citizens experienced war coverage as immediate but overwhelming, with graphic visuals often triggering anxiety. Study 2, a quota-representative survey ( N = 1,000), finds that frequent exposure to such content heightens Austrians’ perceptions of becoming a victim of this war and makes news appear more emotionally unsettling. Together, we demonstrate that cultivation processes persist in today’s fragmented media environment, with important psychological and societal consequences.

item.title: Navigating Precarity: Gendered Labor Inequalities and Economic Vulnerability Among Women Journalists in Ghana
item.dc:creator: Audrey D. Anchirinah, Danford Zirugo
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Audrey D. Anchirinah, Danford Zirugo

Topics: Gender representation, Journalism, Journalistic practice, Professional identity

Women journalists in Ghana navigate a precarious professional environment marked by job insecurity, prolonged unpaid labor, and systemic gender discrimination within a patriarchal society. This study, based on in-depth qualitative interviews with 27 journalists, explores how precarious employment conditions shape their careers and personal lives. Ghanaian women face increased workplace exploitation, harassment, and career stagnation under weak labor protections. This study contributes to broader discussions on journalism precarity in the Global South, highlighting the need for locally grounded perspectives that reflect the unique sociopolitical and economic realities shaping women’s experiences in media.

item.title: Constructing the Journalistic Self: Habitus, Subjectivation, and the Politics of Inequality
item.dc:creator: Vashan Brown
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Vashan Brown

Topics: Journalistic practice, Journalistic roles, Professional identity, Inequality

How do journalists make sense of themselves and their work in postcolonial societies marked by enduring race and class inequalities? This article examines how journalists discursively represent newsroom dynamics, paying particular attention to how their subjectivities are formed. Drawing on 27 semi-structured in-depth interviews with current and former journalists in Jamaica, this study aims to understand how subjectivation and habitus, shape the ways in which journalists reproduce or contest inequalities. It also examines the professional subjectivities and ideologies that are revealed in the discourse of Jamaican journalists and how they relate to race and class inequalities. Existing work on journalism and inequality has largely focused on questions of voice, whose perspectives are included or excluded, and on how media institutions perpetuate structural inequalities. The findings reveal that journalists’ own subjectivities, social backgrounds, and internalised dispositions shape the way they see themselves and the work that they do. The study identifies a typology of journalistic subjectivities that emerge within postcolonial contexts: the class-conscious journalist, the racially conscious journalist, and the racially neutral journalist.

item.title: Layered Censorship: Platform logics and the governance of taboo in religious Media
item.dc:creator: Efrat Refaeli, Motti Neiger
item.description:
European Journal of Communication · Efrat Refaeli, Motti Neiger

Topics: Platformization, Religious media, Censorship, Taboo

This article examines how the governance of taboo issues is reconfigured across platformized communication environments. Drawing on a qualitative comparative analysis of the Walder affair—a moral crisis in Israeli Ultra-Orthodox society that erupted in November 2021 and culminated in the subject's suicide in December of that year—it analyzes how five distinct communication arenas managed allegations of sexual abuse against a prominent religious figure. The findings demonstrate that censorship does not operate as a unified institutional mechanism but as a distributed configuration of communicative practices. Different arenas adopted distinct modes of managing taboo information: institutional silence, normative enforcement, discursive displacement, selective disclosure, and contested openness. These variations reflect the communicative logics, institutional arrangements, and participation structures associated with different communication arenas. To account for these dynamics, the article introduces the concept of Layered Censorship: a platform-differentiated configuration of communicative practices through which taboo information is suppressed, displaced, selectively disclosed, morally regulated, and publicly contested across a shared media ecology. The concept highlights how different communication arenas perform distinct regulatory functions while occupying different positions along a continuum of discursive openness. By conceptualizing censorship as a distributed and differentiated form of communicative governance, the article offers a framework applicable beyond religious contexts to other highly regulated communication environments.

item.title: The Bio-Functional Audience: Shared Physiological Alignment to Narrative Media
item.dc:creator: Ralf Schmälzle, Hee Jung Cho, Monique Mitchell Turner
item.description:
Communication Research · Ralf Schmälzle, Hee Jung Cho, Monique Mitchell Turner

Topics: Message effects, Media effects, Narrative persuasion, Eye-tracking

Communication research into audience responses has traditionally emphasized how individual or group differences create variance in interpretation while overlooking a more fundamental phenomenon: the capacity of the same message to induce similar responses across receivers. We introduce a bio-functional definition of the audience, a temporal collective bound together by the moment-to-moment alignment of its members’ physiological responses. In a large-scale experiment ( N = 198) monitoring eye-tracking, heart rate, and electrodermal activity during a film, we mapped a processing hierarchy in which audience response alignment was strongest for gaze but also extended into downstream autonomic responses. Furthermore, a temporal manipulation of the narrative sequence abolished aligned responses, confirming that the induced audience state is driven by the message content. We conclude that messages function as alignment devices that reduce individual noise and bring distinct individuals into a shared processing state, thus providing a grounded, signal-based definition of the audience as a bio-functional entity.

item.title: Learning the Limits of Belonging: Classroom-Newsroom Gender Paradox in Nigerian Journalism
item.dc:creator: Success N. Osayi, Chioma Charity Agboh, Samson Ighiegba Omosotomhe
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Success N. Osayi, Chioma Charity Agboh, Samson Ighiegba Omosotomhe

Topics: Gender representation, Journalism education, Journalistic practice, Journalism studies

We examine women’s dominance in Nigerian journalism classrooms despite their lack of commensurate representation in newsrooms. Drawing on 27 in-depth interviews with female students, we find that journalism is often pursued as a fallback option, limiting initial motivation. Within training institutions, perceptions of poor teaching, lack of practical training, and toxic learning environments appear to contribute to disengagement from the practice. Patriarchal norms, including assumptions about men’s provider role and privileging men’s authority, shape their perception of these discouraging lessons. The findings compound existing pipeline explanations for this disparity, with implications for scholarship on gender equity, journalism pedagogy, and practice.

item.title: Comparing media systems in the digital age: A longitudinal research based on fuzzy set ideal type analysis
item.dc:creator: Liang Wang, Kunjie Sun
item.description:
European Journal of Communication · Liang Wang, Kunjie Sun

Topics: Media systems, Comparative media research, Media theory, Digital media

Although research on media systems has empirically examined the three media system models proposed in Hallin and Mancini's landmark book Comparing Media Systems, longitudinal comparisons and ideal-type-oriented studies remain rare. These gaps limit scholars’ ability to observe how media systems evolve, particularly in the digital age, and to assess countries’ model membership and degrees of alignment. To fill these gaps, this study applied fuzzy set ideal type analysis to conduct a longitudinal comparison of the 18 countries included in Comparing Media Systems from 2010 to 2023. The findings reveal distinct variants of the classical models in the digital era, trace changes in countries’ ideal-type membership and degrees of alignment over time, and identify a representative case for each model.

item.title: Music Was My First Love: Biographic Resonance Makes Everyday Music Listening Meaningful
item.dc:creator: Felix Dietrich, Alicia Ernst, Benedikt Rohr, Michael Scharkow, Leonard Reinecke
item.description:
Communication Research · Felix Dietrich, Alicia Ernst, Benedikt Rohr, Michael Scharkow, Leonard Reinecke

Topics: Well-being, Media psychology, Music listening, Eudaimonic entertainment

Despite much research on eudaimonic media experiences, little is known about how and why certain content is perceived as meaningful by certain users in certain situations. We therefore examine biographic resonance — connections between entertainment content and users’ biographic memories — during everyday music listening on Spotify and propose that memory recall, as well as its emotional valence, relate to meaningfulness via distinct patterns of intrinsic need satisfaction. Results from a preregistered, intensive-longitudinal study (144 persons; 6,920 situations) reveal that biographic resonance relates to both high- and low-effort modes of eudaimonic entertainment. Moreover, by linking users’ self-reports with their tracked digital music use (2,786 sessions; 107,147 songs), we find that the occurrence and quality of biographic resonance vary across situations and are shaped by both content and contextual factors within algorithmically curated environments. Our results highlight how resonances between media users’ selves and entertainment content foster situational meaningfulness in everyday life.

item.title: Rethinking platform vernaculars: Collective practices and power dynamics in platform environments
item.dc:creator: Lydia Kollyri
item.description:
New Media & Society · Lydia Kollyri

Topics: Platform studies, Platform affordances, Social media use, Digital communication

In 2015, Gibbs et al. introduced the concept of platform vernaculars to describe how communicative genres emerge through interactions between platform affordances and user practices. Although widely adopted in media research, the concept has not been systematically refined in light of recent developments in affordance theory and platform studies. Drawing on an integrative literature review, this paper revisits platform vernaculars as plural, recognizable, repeatable, temporarily stabilized, and contested formations emerging through collective negotiations of affordances within platform environments. The paper further introduces four heuristic categories–intended vernaculars, dominant vernaculars, community vernaculars, and counter-public vernaculars–to discuss how communicative norms, genres, and modes of participation become normalized, marginalized, contested, or transformed across platforms. By rethinking platform vernaculars, the paper offers a systematic analytical framework for studying platform practices and norms. Furthermore, it positions vernaculars as a lens for analyzing platform power and user agency, opening avenues for future research.

item.title: Free Smartphones? But Still Finding It Difficult to Find Place for Phones in Their Lives: Understanding Digital Interactions of Older Widow Women in Rural India
item.dc:creator: Sanju Kumawat, Chhavi Garg
item.description:
Mobile Media & Communication · Sanju Kumawat, Chhavi Garg

Topics: Digital inequality, Intersectionality, Older adults, Digital literacy

This study is an exploration of the digital interactions of older widowed women living in rural India, who received free smartphones under a government scheme aimed at empowering marginalized women. Situated within the intersectionality framework, the research is an analysis of how the interplay of age, gender, widowhood, and rural residence shapes these women’s experiences with technology. Based on semistructured interviews with 16 widowed women aged 60–85 years, it was found in the study that the majority of the respondents are not using the smartphones themselves but have passed on the smartphones to younger female family members, citing utility to younger members and sociocultural norms. The study highlights the complex dynamics of digital inclusion in the Global South, where sociocultural factors lead to expectations that women conform to stereotypes about gender, age, and social status (being widowed) and, hence, significantly influence the adoption and use of technology. The study underscores the need for customized digital literacy initiatives that address both technical skills and the cultural stigmas surrounding technology use among older women living in rural areas. The study contributes to the discourse on the digital divide by focusing on a group that embodies several marginalities, offering insights for policy frameworks aimed at equitable digital empowerment.

item.title: AI Brain Fry: How Artificial Intelligence Is Reshaping Human Cognition at Work
item.dc:creator: Brenda K. Wiederhold
item.description:
Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking · Brenda K. Wiederhold

Topics: Artificial intelligence, Human-AI interaction, Cognitive processing, Digital well-being

item.title: Aspirational technologies of the (disabled) self: Confessional, self-examinatory, and ascetic masculinities among food delivery riders on China’s digital platforms
item.dc:creator: Hao Liang, Zhongxuan Lin
item.description:
New Media & Society · Hao Liang, Zhongxuan Lin

Topics: Digital labor, Digital platforms, Masculinity, Disability

Digital platforms are increasingly offering new employment and social participation opportunities for people with disabilities (PWDs). This study examines the intersections of digital platforms, disability, and masculinity in China. Drawing on in-depth interviews and ethnography with 12 disabled male food delivery riders, it explores how platform-based delivery work serves as a site to negotiate masculinity and social recognition. The findings indicate that platforms not only offer relatively accessible and flexible income opportunities, enabling participants to engage in socially valued work and gendered responsibility, but also mobilize aspirational discourses that promise future inclusion and moral recognition while demanding intensified temporal discipline, bodily endurance, and the willingness to “eat bitterness.” Thus, digital platforms constitute an ambivalent space where inclusion and constraint coexist, enabling gendered self-formation while introducing new forms of discipline. Ultimately, this study calls for greater attention to the challenges faced by PWDs in digital labor.

item.title: Learning the algorithm: Responsibilization and the limits of agency on YouTube
item.dc:creator: Nadia Urban
item.description:
New Media & Society · Nadia Urban

Topics: Platform affordances, Social media algorithms, Algorithmic curation, Social media influencers

Content creators invest extensive effort in “learning the algorithm” to secure visibility and growth. While existing research documents the proliferation of folk theories and optimization strategies, less attention has been paid to the structural conditions under which such learning unfolds. Drawing on a computational analysis of 179 YouTube videos discussing the platform’s algorithm, this article identifies recurring interpretive patterns that frame visibility as optimizable through metrics, strategic adjustment, and disciplined self-management. This paper argues that attempts at algorithmic learning are sustained by an asymmetry between epistemic agency – the capacity to interpret metrics and hypothesize about system behavior, and effective agency – the capacity to reliably influence outcomes. Because large-scale machine-learning systems are probabilistic, multi-objective, and continuously recalibrated, effective control remains systemically indeterminate. This asymmetry produces governance through responsibilization: creators internalize responsibility for unstable outcomes, sustaining engagement because the system appears responsive while remaining structurally uncontrollable.

item.title: Whiteness and the ‘not-so-other’: Ukrainian refugees’ media self-representation in the UK
item.dc:creator: Yael Gordon
item.description:
European Journal of Communication · Yael Gordon

Topics: Social media, Media representation, Media framing, Social identity

This study examines the role of ‘whiteness’ in shaping the experiences of Ukrainian refugees in the UK, focusing on their self-representation on social media. The Ukrainian refugee crisis is portrayed in the media in ways that position Ukrainians as ‘like’ Europeans and as deserving of better treatment from host societies. Cultural proximity influences perceptions of refugees, who are often represented as the Other to Western modernity. Drawing on 50 Facebook posts and images, as well as interviews with 25 refugees living in temporary accommodation in the UK, the study finds that their online self-portrayals and reflections avoid the refugee label and show that they do not perceive themselves as refugees. The research demonstrates how Ukrainian refugees negotiate identity online in ways shaped by the media's power to frame whiteness and cultural proximity, rather than by conventional constructions of refugeehood, while still often aligning with distinctions and hierarchies evident in media portrayals of refugees.

item.title: The narrative construction of disinformation: Reach and impact in Central and Eastern Europe
item.dc:creator: Dren Gërguri, Jaume Suau, Dinko Gruhonjić
item.description:
European Journal of Communication · Dren Gërguri, Jaume Suau, Dinko Gruhonjić

Topics: Disinformation, Narrative persuasion, Political polarization, Media trust

This study analyzes the reach and impact of disinformation narratives within four Central-Eastern Europe countries: the Czech Republic, Kosovo, Poland, and Serbia. Using survey data collected in mid-2023, we examine how citizens have been exposed to common disinformation narratives (reach) and how this prior exposure influences their belief in them (impact). The results provide empirical information on this underrepresented area, which highlights that the repeated, reinforcing impact of previous exposure is a universal cognitive mechanism. This study contributes to the literature in two significant ways. In theory, they demonstrate the value of shifting from a claim-based to a narrative-based paradigm, which is much more similar to the clustering, emotional appeal, and ideological framing of disinformation. The findings provide empirical evidence from an underrepresented region in the study of disinformation, demonstrating how foreign-sponsored and domestically produced narratives hijack all of those concerns and exploit existing political divisions, historical grievances, and media weaknesses.

item.title: Platformed Care: Gender and Care Mobilities Across Ride-Hailing Platforms
item.dc:creator: Mónica Humeres, Catalina Alarcon, Jacqueline Vega-Poblete
item.description:
Mobile Media & Communication · Mónica Humeres, Catalina Alarcon, Jacqueline Vega-Poblete

Topics: Platformization, Digital platforms, Gender differences, Digital labor

This article examines how ride-hailing platforms mediate care mobility in everyday contexts, focusing on women-only and mixed-gender services in Chile. Drawing on 37 qualitative interviews with users and drivers, the study shows that caregiving responsibilities are an important yet underexamined reason women engage with these platforms, highlighting the gendered organization of care-related mobility. Participants use apps to coordinate children's routines, assist elderly relatives, and manage everyday travel with limited time, resources, and support. The findings show that these practices extend beyond transport. Women drivers often perform additional unremunerated forms of care, including waiting beyond scheduled times, offering emotional support, and assisting dependents. These interactions reveal how platform-mediated mobility operates across blurred boundaries between paid service and informal care, shaped by gendered expectations around responsibility and care. The article introduces the concept of platformed care to describe how mobile media and mobility platforms are used to coordinate and delegate caregiving-related mobility under conditions of distance and gendered vulnerability. Rather than resolve structural constraints, these platforms reorganize care mobility while reproducing existing inequalities.

item.title: Overconfident youth, underconfident elders: Age differences in algorithmic knowledge confidence and information perceptions
item.dc:creator: Myojung Chung
item.description:
New Media & Society · Myojung Chung

Topics: Algorithmic literacy, Social media algorithms, Age differences, Information credibility

Age-related differences in algorithmic knowledge are typically interpreted as competence gaps that render younger “digital natives” better equipped and older users more vulnerable in algorithmically curated environments. This study challenges these assumptions by examining (a) algorithmic knowledge confidence—whether users’ subjective algorithmic knowledge exceeds or falls short of their algorithmic awareness and knowledge—and (b) what consequences such misalignment has for information environment perceptions. Using US survey data ( N = 1205), this study found systematic misalignment between subjective and awareness-based algorithmic knowledge: younger users overestimate their understanding, whereas older users underestimate theirs. Social media use partially mediated the age–knowledge confidence relationship. Knowledge confidence, in turn, predicted perceived information reliability and diversity. These findings reveal that critical assessment of information environment is determined not by knowledge level alone but by alignment between subjective and awareness-based knowledge, highlighting the need for age-tailored interventions addressing knowledge overconfidence and underconfidence.
